CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the back of the heel and calf.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a first-time patient training for a triathlon (running about 10 kilometers in the morning, biking 45 minutes to an hour at lunchtime, and swimming 30 minutes to an hour in the evening, 5 days a week, with a long run and long bike on weekends and 1 day off). He reports pain in the back of his heel typically after a workout or when first getting up in the morning, extending all the way up into his calf. The doctor suggests it could be plantar fasciitis initially, but later diagnoses achilles tendinitis from overuse. 

The patient does not stretch at all before running or biking. When he first gets out of bed, it feels really tight and almost like it's tearing; it eases up after walking for 10 or 15 minutes, but gets really sore again after sitting for an extended period and trying to get back up, or after a lot of activity. The pain is mainly on the right side; his left leg does not hurt.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Lower extremities examined. 
- Right foot and ankle: Pulling toes up toward him creates a little bit of pain. Pushing against the doctor's hand also hurts a little bit.
- Squeezing left calf: No pain on the left side.
- Squeezing right calf: No pain. Thompson test is negative.
- Squeezing right heel: Causes significant pain.
- Palpation further up the right achilles tendon: Real tender.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Diagnosis: Achilles tendinitis, from overuse.
- Activity modification: The doctor asks the patient to stop training for a week or two to let it heal.
- Medications: Take ibuprofen or advil, three tablets every six hours as an anti-inflammatory.
- Physical therapy: The doctor will order a couple of physical therapy visits for strength and stretching understanding, and to learn how to stretch muscles before activities and strengthen lower extremities.
- Imaging: No x-ray indicated at this point; however, if significant pain continues after 10 days without activity modification, more aggressive treatment plans may be considered.
- Follow-up: Return in 7 to 10 days following the first couple of physical therapy appointments to monitor progress.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems (depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male presenting for follow-up. 
Regarding his depression, he reports doing pretty well over the last six months. He sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming a lot at the pool. He does not want to start medications at this time and feels no need to, but knows he can call the doctor if he does. The doctor agrees that medication is not needed at this time.
Regarding his hypertension, he states he still has good and bad days and takes his medicine (Norvasc) daily, but admits to occasional burgers, wine, and salt intake. He checks his blood pressure about once a week using a machine at CVS pharmacy.
Regarding his rotator cuff repair from about 8 months ago, he reports it is doing well. He has progressed to home exercises, stretching with a yoga ball, and getting stronger each time.
The patient also notes a little bit of ankle swelling, mainly near the end of the day, which seems to go away by the next morning. He denies nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Positive for a little bit of ankle swelling near the end of the day that goes away by the next morning. Review of systems sheet completed at check-in otherwise noted the patient is doing well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Blood pressure: Elevated today at 156/94. Readings have been running a little high over the past couple of months.
- Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated, which is stable and has been heard in the past.
- Lungs: Sound nice and clear.
- Lower extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.

RESULTS
- Labs: Creatinine (kidney function) looks stable; overall lab results look really good.
- EKG: Looks fine, with no evidence of coronary artery disease; described as a nice, normal EKG.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing really well with management, good strategies, and a good support system. No medication to be started at this time; patient knows he can call if needed.
2. Hypertension: Believed not to be well controlled at this time. Plan to increase Norvasc to 10 mg a day. Order an echocardiogram and a lipid panel. Discussed decreasing salt intake regarding diet and edema.
3. Rotator cuff repair: Doing really well, progressing with home exercises. No further intervention needed; pretty much resolved.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Martin is a 79-year-old female presenting for follow-up. Her recent A1c was 9.9, indicating poorly controlled blood sugar. She has been taking glimepiride 2 mg, which the doctor instructed her to increase to two 2 mg pills twice a day (total 4 mg twice a day) using her current supply, with a new prescription to be written for 4 mg twice a day. She reports trying to eat healthier by avoiding pasta and bread, though she eats two slices of wheat bread in the morning and occasionally peanut butter sandwiches. She drinks club soda and seltzer water rather than regular water or sodas. 

Regarding her eyes, she recently saw Dr. Sanchez at the Liberty Road group for her prescription following cataract surgery and iodine treatment. She notes one lens feels a bit funny, while the other is good. 

For her hypertension, she reports a home reading of 116 a couple of weeks ago, though today's check in the office was 140 over 60. She is taking metoprolol 50 mg once a day, lisinopril with hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg once a day, and amlodipine 10 mg once a day. 

For her high cholesterol and vascular disease, she is taking atorvastatin and tolerating it, though she reports ongoing foot and leg pain ("feet feel like hell") that makes walking difficult. The patient suggests it might be sciatica, while the doctor attributes the foot symptoms to peripheral neuropathy. She also reports pain extending up to her hips and upper legs. 

She continues to smoke and is not ready to quit.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Feeling totally normal. No fever or chills.
Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat: No headaches or dizziness. Vision is improved with cataract surgery, though one lens feels funny. Coughing lately due to congestion with relatively clear sputum.
Cardiovascular: No chest pains, pressure, or tightness.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or other GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Slower stream, but stable; gets up to pee once in a while at night, noting she tends to drink fluids in the evening.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Carotids: Normal, pulse without bruits.
Heart: Rhythm is regular, normal rate, S1 and S2 are crisp, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear, no rasps or wheezes.
Extremities: Without edema. Pulses are palpable on dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. Thickened nails, mildly dry skin, no skin breakdown. 
Neurological: Mildly decreased sensation in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Poorly controlled (A1c 9.9). Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day (take two 2 mg pills twice a day of current supply; new prescription will be for 4 mg twice a day). Continue metformin. Watch for signs of low blood sugar (weakness, shakiness, sweating).
2. Peripheral Neuropathy: Mildly decreased sensation in toes and foot pain. Advise keeping feet moisturized; patient plans to use a foot scrub or cream.
3. Hypertension: Office BP 140/60 (home readings reported better). Continue current combination of metoprolol, lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide, and amlodipine. Check kidney function via labs today.
4. Hyperlipidemia / Vascular Disease: Continue atorvastatin.
5. Tobacco Use: Patient continues to smoking; discussed quitting, but patient is not ready.
6. Labs: Order blood work today to check blood sugar/A1c and kidney function.
7. Follow-up: Return in four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up from an emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an ER visit. He reports that while playing tennis on Saturday in very hot and humid weather, he experienced severe shortness of breath and breathing struggle after about half an hour. He thought he was having a heart attack, got very nervous, and his wife took him to the ER. Everything checked out there, but he was very upset about it. The doctor wonders if it might have been heat exhaustion. About six hours after getting home from the ER, the patient felt very lightheaded and very dizzy. On Sunday, he felt fine, but thought it was worth checking up with the doctor. He reports taking all of his heart failure medications diligently and staying in touch with his doctor. Regarding his diet, he admits he cheats every now and then with salty foods and junk food, though he mostly does a good job avoiding them. He also notes that his cataract surgery from three months ago and his skin cancer removal from five months ago have both healed nicely with no ongoing problems.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for vision problems. No other systems reviewed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Very supple, no jugular venous distention noted (transcript notes "fibular venous distention").
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur. Blood pressure is a little high (noted to be high in the ER as well).
Lungs: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy, which caused his congestive heart failure.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low, but stable.
Skin Biopsy / Pathology Report: Shows they got all of the skin cancer and everything is fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath / Congestive heart failure exacerbation: The doctor believes the ER visit for shortness of breath was an exacerbation of heart failure, likely provoked by dietary indiscretion (eating salty food leading to fluid retention). 
   - Prescribe an extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once a day.
   - Start Carvedilol 25 mg twice a day.
2. Cataract surgery and skin cancer removal: Both are doing well; no medication adjustments needed.
3. Blood pressure: Noted to be elevated; to be monitored.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male presenting for evaluation of a lower back injury that occurred about four months ago while moving boxes. The patient thinks it might be a pulled muscle. He tried some physical therapy at his gym, which did not seem to help. Initially, for a very short period, he felt like he was going to topple over and could not support his upper body weight, and the toes on his right foot tingled a little bit, but that went away after about an hour and has not happened since. He reports feeling nervous about carrying something heavy due to leg sensations, but notes normal leg strength otherwise. He still has pain in his lower back if he turns a certain way or rolls over in his sleep, which wakes him with a sharp pain that resolves with repositioning. He has taken Tylenol, ibuprofen (which works a little better for a shorter period), tried heat, and tried ice, with no real relief. He did not get stomach upset from ibuprofen. He previously went to an urgent care where an MRI was recommended, but he did not get it due to insurance concerns and because he started to feel better; however, because symptoms have persisted, he now wants to move forward with it. He denies any bladder or bowel incontinence or difficulty. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever or chills. Denies bladder or bowel incontinence or difficulty going to the bathroom. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Temperature normal, blood pressure 117/56, heart rate 68, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance of C5-C6 appreciated; no pain to touch.
Lumbar spine: No pain to palpation of the lumbar spine. Decreased flexion and extension of the lower back. Positive straight leg raise. Spasm of the paraspinal muscles of the lumbar spine.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremities strength is equal bilaterally. 
Other: The doctor noted the patient has some arthritis in the neck and/or a little bit of injury from the back incident.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine x-ray showed no acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute disc herniation (doctor believes this is likely based on ongoing symptoms since the incident a few months ago).
2. Order a lumbar spine MRI to evaluate soft tissues.
3. Continue physical therapy; refer the patient to a physical therapist through the health system.
4. Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once a day for pain and inflammation.
5. Discussed potential future treatment options if a herniated disc is confirmed, such as an epidural steroid injection to reduce inflammation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on it.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elijah is a patient referred by his primary care provider who presents with right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on his foot yesterday while doing yard work. He was able to keep working after the incident, though it became sore and swollen, prompting him to see his doctor. He rates his pain as 11 out of 10 right now. He reports numbness in the whole foot, which he states has been present for a long time. He has not taken any medication for the pain. The patient notes a history of a broken ankle 20 years ago that occasionally gives him trouble and swells, as well as soreness and occasional giving out in his other ankle, which had surgery.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals look good. Focused exam of the right foot shows bruising on the bottom and top parts of the foot, associated swelling, and tenderness to palpation for the midfoot. Neurovascular exam of the right foot shows brisk capillary refill in less than three seconds, a strong bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, and motor and sensation intact for that foot, matching bilaterally.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot shows dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a three-millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases and presence of bony fragments.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Right foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone and the top of the foot).
- The doctor wants to order an MRI to assess for any injuries to ligaments in the foot. The doctor plans to send the order to the outpatient MRI facility downstairs to get the MRI done this afternoon.
- Based on the exam and x-ray, the patient is most likely going to need surgery to allow bones and ligaments to heal properly and prevent losing the arch, becoming flat-footed, and developing arthritis. Surgery would involve putting bones back into place using plates and screws.
- Surgery would be an outpatient procedure (same day, discharged home that evening), proposed for tomorrow if the patient is agreeable.
- Post-procedure plan: follow-up in 24 hours and again in two weeks. The patient would be in a cast, use crutches, and be non-weight-bearing for six to eight weeks, with gradual advancement of ambulating based on healing and tolerance.
- The patient asked about staying in a cast instead of surgery and asked about the timing of the MRI; the patient ultimately stated he would like to think about it and have some time.

Right-sided back pain and blood in urine, evaluated for kidney stone.

She also started to see some blood in her urine. She reports no real pain when urinating. She took some ibuprofen which helped a little bit, but it still hurts. She has not thrown up, but has felt a little bit nauseated. She had some pain over the weekend (Easter break) and saw her PCP this morning, who sent her over due to concern for a kidney stone. This is her first time having kidney stones. Her father had kidney stones and she thinks he has passed a couple of them. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
- Constitutional: No fever or chills reported; felt a little bit nauseated, no vomiting.
- Genitourinary: Blood in urine observed; no pain with urination.
- Musculoskeletal: Right-sided back pain moving to the right lower side.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vitals: Vitals look good; no fever, blood pressure and heart rate are fine.
- Abdomen: Mild pain and tenderness to palpation of the abdomen. No rebound or guarding.
- Flank/Back: CVA (costovertebral angle) located near the flank tenderness on the right. 

RESULTS
- CT scan of the side: Showed a stone measuring 0.5 cm in size located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis (not obstructing the ureter causing swelling in the kidney).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Assessment: Kidney stone on the right, 0.5 cm in the proximal right ureter, with what seems to be some inflammation of the kidney.

  - Based on urinalysis results, the doctor will decide if antibiotics are needed for an infection.
  - Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. If still having symptoms, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy (a minimally invasive procedure using shock waves to break up the stone).

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Lawrence is a 62-year-old male with a past medical history of type I diabetes, congestive heart failure, depression, and reflux, who presents with complaints of shortness of breath. The shortness of breath has been going on for about 10 days. The patient notices it when walking up a flight of stairs. He also reports swelling up a little bit in his legs and feeling really lethargic. The patient thinks a lot of it has to do with going to some house parties and eating some salty foods. The doctor wonders if it might be a kidney problem. 

The patient reports feeling a little uncomfortable and pretty stiff when waking up in the morning, taking a little while to adjust to walking. He woke up acutely short of breath once, about a week ago, but it has not happened since, so he has not been concerned about it. 

Regarding his type I diabetes, he monitors it during the working week using an insulin pump, but on Saturdays and Sundays he gets busy and forgets to monitor it, though he has not seen any spikes. He admits to loving chocolate bars. 

Regarding his depression, the patient states it has been a crazy year and a half. He tried natural solutions like outdoor stretches in the summer, but the weather changed and he is looking for alternatives. He is not ready to try medications just yet and is open to suggestions. He denies any suicidal or homicidal ideation ("no issues with your depression? you do n't want to hurt yourself or anyone else? ... no. no. absolutely not."). 

Regarding reflux, he is on omeprazole and has been making lifestyle modifications by cutting back on Red Bull and caffeine. Alcohol intake was tough during the holiday season, but he is better.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
The patient endorsed shortness of breath. He denied chest pain, fever, chills, cough, and belly pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs in the office look good, and pulse oximetry looks good while sitting.
Neck: No jugular venous distension or carotid bruits appreciated.
Heart: Slight 3 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated.
Lungs: Crackles appreciated bilaterally at the bases.
Lower extremities: 1+ pitting edema appreciated.

RESULTS
Chest X-ray: Reviewed, looks good. No evidence of any airspace disease and no pneumonia.
Labs: White blood cell count is not elevated; no concern for infection.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath / Acute heart failure exacerbation: Thought to be retaining some fluid, likely from dietary indiscretion. 
- Prescribe Lasix 40 milligrams a day.
- Weigh daily; if weight is not going down or is going up, call the doctor.
- If more short of breath at rest, call the doctor or call 911 and go to the emergency room; might need intravenous diuretics.

2. Type I diabetes:
- Order a hemoglobin A1c in about a month to see if adjustments are needed.
- Follow up with the endocrinologist.
- Ensure a recent eye exam is done.

3. Depression:
- Refer to psychiatry for talk therapy to help through it (no medications).

4. Reflux:
- Continue omeprazole 20 milligrams a day.

Newly diagnosed hypercholesterolemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Julie Cruz is a 17-year-old non-binary emancipated minor with no significant past medical history who presents for evaluation of newly diagnosed hypercholesterolemia. The patient reports having a finger-prick cholesterol test at an annual checkup that came back elevated, prompting the referral. The patient wonders if it might be diabetes. 

The patient stays active during the week, riding a bicycle on trails and going for bike rides with friends. Regarding diet, the patient reports liking chocolate chip cookies and trying to cook mostly fresh food and eat a clean diet most days, and expresses surprise at the high cholesterol finding. Last year, the patient had cholesterol checked and it was noted to be a little borderline, but the previous doctor blew it off and told the patient to watch what they were eating.

The patient does not talk to parents much and does not know of any early-age hypercholesterolemia in the parents. The patient has a good relationship with grandparents; both grandparents reported that when they were young they did not have anything like that. The patient reports a family history where a cousin died at around 44 or 45 years old, and the grandparents think he had a heart attack. 

The patient lives on their own, and nobody in the patient's apartment or among friends smokes. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Growing okay, feels healthy, living as nongender for about two years. 
Cardiovascular: No history of early heart disease or sudden death known in parents or grandparents, aside from a cousin who died at age 44 or 45 from a suspected heart attack.
All other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure looks good.
Heart: No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear.
Eyes: No xanthelasmas.
Neck: No thyromegaly.
Abdomen: No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.

RESULTS
Cholesterol level was elevated at 210 (high).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Newly diagnosed hypercholesterolemia / elevated cholesterol (cholesterol level 210).
- The doctor notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends all children be screened between ages 9 and 11 and again between ages 17 and 20, and that studies show a link between high cholesterol and premature heart attacks.
- Order a full cholesterol panel.
- Check glucose, complete metabolic panel (CMP), thyroid studies, and liver panels to look for secondary causes.
- Perform genetic testing to see if the problem is familial or has a secondary cause.
- Follow a well-balanced diet including a variety of foods lower in saturated fat and sugars.
- Meet with a nutritionist for information about what foods to eat.
- Continue physical activity and exercise, specifically bike riding.
- Follow up with another cholesterol level in 3 to 6 months after meeting with the nutritionist and instituting dietary changes.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Low back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male who presents with real bad low back pain that started a couple of weeks ago while lifting a box of books, during which he felt a pop. The patient wonders if it might be a pulled muscle and notes he probably did not use proper lifting technique. The pain is described as achy and sharp in the low back. Initially the pain did not radiate, but now the patient feels it starting to shoot down his left leg. Sitting is usually okay. The patient reports no numbness, tingling, loss of sensation, or weakness. He denies any loss of control of his bladder or bowels. He tried taking ibuprofen and Tylenol, which sometimes helps. Surgery has not been discussed previously. His activity level includes trying to exercise a few times a week, though he is pretty inconsistent and has a sedentary job. The pain has made him feel like he does not want to be as active as he was previously, though it has not affected his job. Family history is positive for back pain in his father. He does not smoke and has a history of playing soccer as a midfielder.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Not discussed.
Eyes: Not discussed.
Ears, Nose, Throat: Not discussed.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Lungs sound clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Gastrointestinal: Denies loss of bowel control.
Genitourinary: Denies loss of bladder control.
Musculoskeletal: Low back pain, shooting pain down the left leg, midline tenderness, pain with lumbar flexion. Denies weakness.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation. Patella and achilles reflexes are symmetrical. Left-sided radiating pain.
Skin: No overlying redness or bruising on the skin.
Endocrine: Not discussed.
Hematologic/Lymphatic: Not discussed.
Allergic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure in the 130/70 range, respiratory rate 18.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal/Back: No overlying redness or bruising on the skin. Midline tenderness at the L4-L5 disc space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Able to bend forward and backward; bending forward causes pain (pain with lumbar flexion).
Supine straight leg test: Positive.
Neurological: No decreased sensation to touch. Patella and achilles reflexes are symmetrical.

RESULTS
MRI shows disc desiccation, a disc bulge with paracentral disc herniation resulting in moderate right neural foraminal stenosis, indicating a herniated disc with nerve impingement.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Lumbar back pain at the L4-L5 disc space due to a herniated disc with radiculopathy.
Plan: 
- Recommend a spinal injection with a strong NSAID and a corticosteroid into the lumbar spine under fluoroscopy (x-ray) to help with inflammation.
- Schedule the procedure to be done today.
- Provide paperwork with explanations of risks and complications for the patient to review, with opportunity for further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Numbness and tingling in the right hand.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an administrative worker who sits at a keyboard all day and reports numbness and tingling in the right hand, mostly affecting the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. The symptoms have been present on and off for about six months and have become more persistent over the last month. The patient reports some pain, mostly when typing on the keyboard and when using the mouse. The patient notes that stopping typing and resting help the most, and reports taking ibuprofen for pain. The pain does not wake the patient up in the middle of the night and does not affect sleep. The doctor mentions it might be a pinched nerve.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Examination of the right hand shows pain on wrist extension and flexion. Decreased grip strength is noted on the right side. Tapping on the inside of the wrist/forearm causes a grimace and shooting pain (positive Tinel's sign).

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Carpal tunnel syndrome (doctor's opinion). 
Plan: 
- Provide a wrist splint to be worn at night.
- Continue ibuprofen, increasing the dose to 600 mg four times a day.
- Order an outpatient EMG (nerve conduction study) of the wrist. 
- Depending on the test results, discuss potential physical therapy or future consideration of a simple outpatient surgery to release the nerve impingement if conservative treatment is unsuccessful.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Breast reduction consult.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 25-year-old female considering a breast reduction, a procedure she has been thinking about for about six or seven years. She experiences neck and upper back pain, which she thinks she could attribute to her breasts when working at her desk all day, and notes the pain has been ongoing since she was in high school. She has been going to a chiropractor for a few years, though the doctor suggests it might be scoliosis. She wears a 34E sports bra and notes bra strap indentations, though she does not wear a regular bra often. She reports sometimes having numbness or tingling in the hands and nipple pain. Her breasts are always sweaty, but she denies rashes underneath them. She states her activities are limited, noting that working out, jumping, and running cause pain and require her to hold them. She takes propranolol for migraines and notes a family history of breast cancer (mother diagnosed at age 40, recommended to start mammograms at age 30, though she has not had any yet). She lost about 10 pounds over the past few months and would like to lose about 20 more pounds. She drinks a little wine on occasion and uses no tobacco or drugs. She is currently studying psychology. Her insurance is currently Blue Cross Blue Shield, but she expects to transition to her husband's new insurance plan most likely in July.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Inspection of the breasts reveals asymmetrical breasts with severe ptosis bilaterally. One breast is a little lower than the other. There is no nipple retraction or discharge bilaterally. No breast tenderness, masses, or axillary lymphadenopathy is palpable. 

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- The patient is a 25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia, presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. 
- The patient has attempted nonsurgical treatments with minimal relief and is an ideal candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty. 
- Minimum required resection, based on a BSA of 2.65 with the Schnur scale, is 1,792 grams, which should be attainable. Given her extremely large breasts and measurements, there is potential for using a nipple graft.
- The patient is a great candidate for a breast reduction to remove tissue, lift the breasts, and elevate the nipple position to help relieve back and neck pain. 
- Surgery details discussed include an anchor-shaped incision, removing extra fat and breast tissue to achieve a smaller size (likely a small C cup, as the doctor explains she can be made as small as blood supply allows without cutting off the nipple's blood supply). Surgery typically takes about three hours.
- Postoperative plan includes drains on each side for about a week to prevent fluid buildup, clear plastic tape over the incision to help with scars (which will be red at first and take about a year to mature), and staying overnight in the hospital for one night for pain and nausea control.
- Discussed potential risks and effects: approximately 30% of patients cannot breastfeed after reduction due to removal of fat and glands; pregnancy hormones and weight changes will alter the breasts over time; nipple sensation is typically fine but there is a slight chance of alteration or loss of sensation; bruising is normal.
- Activity restrictions for about six weeks after surgery include no heavy lifting and no driving for two to three weeks.
- The office will wait until July when the patient is on her new insurance plan to submit for insurance approval. The patient will notify the office as soon as she has the new insurance information.
- Photos will be taken today for documentation and submission to the insurance company. Once approved, the office will work with the patient on a surgery date, and they will meet again prior to surgery.

Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male who presents with right knee pain that began about five days ago while water skiing on Lake Martin. He did a jump and twisted his knee when he landed. He reports no popping sound or sensation, but felt like something stretched, followed by swelling. He was able to get out of the water by himself, though climbing up and any squatting or bending is very sore. This is the first time he has injured this knee. He has been taking over-the-counter Aleve twice a day and using a cold pack, which has helped a fair amount, though the knee remains pretty sore. He reports no numbness or tingling in his foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the foot. Otherwise, review of systems is negative except as noted in the history of present illness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure in the office is 120/77.
Neck: No lymphadenopathy appreciated.
Heart: Nice regular rate and rhythm, no murmur appreciated.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal (Right Knee): Ecchymosis and edema present, effusion present. Pain to palpation of the right medial knee. Decreased range of motion. Negative varus and valgus test. Negative Lachman sign. Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. Otherwise no lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right knee pain: The doctor and patient agree the patient had quite an injury to the knee with fluid and inflammation. The doctor suspects a medial collateral ligament strain (and previously mentioned a torn meniscus as a possible thought, though not sure).
   - Order an x-ray of the right knee to rule out broken bones.
   - Refer to physical therapy to strengthen muscles around the knee.
   - Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once a day for swelling and pain.

2. Hypertension: Well-managed on current regimen.
   - Continue lisinopril 20 mg a day.
   - Order a lipid panel.
3. Health maintenance:
   - Administer a tetanus shot (patient is due).

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
James is a 57-year-old male with a past medical history significant for congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes who presents with back pain. The patient reports he hurt his back on Saturday morning (about four days ago) while golfing when he went for his backswing. He felt a pop and immediately had to hit the ground to try and loosen up his back. The doctor states it might be a pinched nerve, though he is not sure. 

For the pain, the patient took Tylenol, ibuprofen, tried ice, and tried heat, but nothing really worked. By Monday morning, it loosened up a little bit, but it is still pretty sore. The patient reports having a struggle with his right foot like dropped foot and some struggling with his right leg; he felt that for a while, and it got a little bit better this morning, but not much. He is able to walk around a little bit, though not too fast and not doing anything strenuous. The patient has a history of lower back surgery about 10 years ago.

Regarding congestive heart failure, the patient states he has been pretty good taking his medications, watching his diet (avoiding salty foods), and trying to exercise regularly. He reports a little bit of weight gain over the summer, but nothing radical (no more than five pounds). He denies any problems laying flat while going to bed.

Regarding type 2 diabetes, the patient states watching his diet is a struggle because he has a sweet tooth and loves jelly beans, but he is getting through it. He monitors his blood sugar regularly at home, though he can sometimes forget, and he is still taking metformin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
The nurse did a review of systems sheet when the patient checked in, where the patient endorsed back pain and maybe a little weakness in his right leg. All other symptoms were negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look great and completely normal in the office.
General/Heart: A 2 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur is appreciated, which has been heard in the past and is stable.
Back: Pain to palpation of the lumbar spine at the level of L5. Decreased range of motion with flexion and extension. Positive straight leg raise.
Strength: 4 out of 5 on the right and 5 out of 5 on the left.

RESULTS
Back X-ray: Normal X-ray of the lumbar spine. Good bony alignment with no abnormality seen, which is not surprising based on the history.
Diabetic labs: Hemoglobin A1c has been a little high at 8 (the doctor would like to see that a little bit lower around 7).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute lumbar strain: The doctor thinks the patient probably injured his back with a muscle strain. 
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 milligrams once a day.
- Refer to physical therapy to strengthen the area.
- If the patient is still having symptoms, order an MRI to make sure there is no disc herniation or anything like that.
- Follow up in a couple of weeks.

2. Type 2 diabetes: 
- Increase metformin to 1,000 milligrams twice daily.
- Order another hemoglobin A1c in a couple of months.

3. Congestive heart failure: The doctor thinks the patient is doing really well with it.
- Continue current medications, including lisinopril and Lasix.
- Order a refill of lisinopril 20 milligrams once a day.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Breast reduction consultation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Julia Jones is a 25-year-old female presenting for a breast reduction consultation, which she has been considering for about six or seven years (since high school). She has been seeing a chiropractor for a few years for pain in her neck and upper back/shoulders, which she attributes to her breasts when working at her desk all day, though she also notes it might be scoliosis. She wears a 34E sports bra (estimates her size at a G cup) due to comfort and cost, and experiences bra strap indentations. She reports occasional numbness or tingling in the hands and occasional nipple pain. She denies rashes under her breasts, though she notes they are always sweaty. She reports that activities such as working out, jumping, and running are limited because her breasts hurt and she has to hold them. She has not tried physical therapy and does not take pain medicine for her back, but takes propranolol for migraines. She has no children now, but might plan to in the future. She has a family history of breast cancer (mother diagnosed at age 40, recommended to start mammograms at age 30, though she is currently 25 and has not had one). She lost about 10 pounds over the past few months and would like to lose about 20 more pounds. She drinks a little wine on occasion and does not use tobacco or drugs. She has Blue Cross Blue Shield insurance currently, but expects to switch to her husband's new insurance plan (not Blue Cross) most likely in July, at which point she plans to submit for insurance approval.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Healthy, for the most part; lost 10 pounds recently.
Breasts: Heavy breasts, severe ptosis, bra strap indentations, occasional nipple pain, sweaty, occasional numbness or tingling in the hands. Pain/limitations with jumping, running, and working out. Denies rashes underneath the breasts.
Musculoskeletal: Neck and upper back/shoulder pain since high school.
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: 25-year-old female, new breast reduction consult.
Breasts: Inspection reveals asymmetrical breasts (one breast is a little lower than the other) with severe ptosis bilaterally. No nipple retraction or discharge bilaterally. No breast tenderness, masses, or axillary lymphadenopathy is palpable. Measurements taken.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- The patient is a 25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia, presenting for evaluation of breast reduction.
- She has attempted nonsurgical treatments with minimal relief, and is an ideal candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty.
- Her minimum required resection, based on a BSA of 2.65 with the Schnur scale, is 1,792 grams, which should be attainable. Given her extremely large breasts and measurements, there is potential for using a nipple graft.
- Discussed surgical procedure: removal of fat and breast tissue, lifting and elevating the nipple position, anchor-shaped incision (around the nipple, straight down, and underneath), and potential final size of a small C cup (aiming to be as small as blood supply allows).
- Discussed surgery details: typically takes about three hours, one night stay in the hospital for pain control and nausea monitoring, drains in each side for about a week, clear plastic tape over incisions, and red scars initially that take about a year to mature.
- Discussed risks and considerations: approximately 30% of patients cannot breastfeed afterward depending on the amount of fat and gland removed; breasts will change over time with weight fluctuation or pregnancy; slight chance of altered or absent nipple sensation (though generally fine unless a massive reduction); bruising which resolves over time; activity restrictions for about six weeks (no heavy lifting, no driving for two to three weeks).
- Plan to wait until July when the patient's insurance switches to her husband's new plan, then submit photographs and documentation for insurance approval. 
- Catherine will come in to take photos today.
- The patient will notify the office as soon as she has the new insurance information to proceed with submission, after which a surgery date will be scheduled and a pre-surgery meeting will be held.

Diagnostic imaging review: Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3-millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

- Based on the exam and x-ray, the patient is most likely going to need surgery. Surgery will place the bones back in their proper position using plates and screws to hold them while they heal, allowing bones and ligaments to heal properly. It is a day surgery and the patient will go home the same day.
- Risk of not performing surgery: Significant complications including poor bone and ligament healing leading to loss of the foot arch, becoming flat-footed, and a high likelihood of developing arthritis in the foot.
- Follow-up: Patient will follow up with the doctor in the clinic on Monday morning. The patient will be in a cast, will need to use crutches, and will not be able to use the left foot for about 6 to 8 weeks. After 6 to 8 weeks, the patient will gradually start walking on the foot based on tolerance. 
- Patient will be out for the rest of the soccer season.
- Nurse will provide paperwork to get started.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Heart failure and recent hospitalization.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents following a recent hospitalization for heart failure. She reports she was doing better now, but previously experienced ankle swelling that would not go down even when going to bed, and had trouble breathing requiring her to be propped up in bed at night. She had a hard time talking, and a friend (Diane) suggested calling 911. An ambulance took her to the ER. The doctor thinks the event could possibly be pneumonia. 

The patient's blood pressure was noted to be high at 200/90 in the hospital. Regarding medications, the patient states she might miss one now and then, but tries to take them all the time. Regarding diet, the patient admits to eating salty foods, specifically brand-name salt and vinegar potato chips, probably every day as home snacking. 

Since being in the hospital and receiving a "water pill" (bumex), the patient feels better, has less shortness of breath (which she thinks is helped by walking a little more), though the water pill causes almost incontinence. An additional blood pressure medication was added, and she feels a little better with it if she can remember to take the pills. The doctor suggested a pill box or phone alarm to help with medication adherence. The patient already owns a home blood pressure cuff and will try to use it every day now and keep a log of blood pressures and food intake. Since coming home, she has had no shortness of breath or sleeping problems (sleeping like a log), and no chest pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure: 128/72
Temperature: 98.7
Heart rate: 72
Respirations: 18
Oxygen saturation: 96%
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated (noted as previously heard and stable).
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Lower extremities: Trace edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved ejection fraction (EF) of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: Caused by dietary indiscretion and some uncontrolled hypertension. 
- Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily.
- Continue to watch diet and avoid salty foods.
- Keep a log of blood pressures and what has been eaten if blood pressure seems high.
- Weigh daily and call the doctor if weight gain is 3 pounds in 2 days.
- See a nutritionist for food education.

2. Hypertension: 
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order a renal artery ultrasound to rule out renal artery stenosis or other issues.

3. Kidney disease: 
- Get more labs to ensure tolerance of the new medications.
- Follow-up visit in three months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Heart murmur and fatigue.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ISSUES
Diana Scott is a 100-year-old female presenting as a new patient for evaluation of a new, worrisome heart murmur reported by her doctor. She is unsure how big the murmur is or what it is. She reports she does not think she has any symptoms, though she notes she does not move as fast as she used to. She denies chest pain. She reports severe pain in her legs for about a month, for which she started taking pain pills, and had a chest x-ray last week. She reports feeling short of breath if she walks too fast or too long, or if she tries to drink a whole glass of water without stopping. The doctor wonders if this might be anemia. She uses a walker and can walk to the end of the driveway or around the cul-de-sac before feeling short of breath or overly fatigued. She states it is not that bothersome unless she tries to overdo it. She states her symptoms are about 70% to 80% different compared to about six months ago, noting she did not notice anything at all before that. She reports her legs have been severe for about a month and that seems to limit her. She reports feeling lightheaded or dizzy and takes a pill (meclizine) for it when it gets bad, not every day. She denies passing out. She denies irregular heartbeats, feeling like her heart is going too fast, or skipping a beat. She reports her ankles swell, which has been going on for probably six months, going up and down and sometimes worse than other times. She reports she lost a little bit of weight, weighing 120 pounds now compared to her normal weight of 130 pounds, going down gradually for about a year. She denies fevers or chills. She reports she came in mostly because of the murmur and because she feels overly tired from taking all her medication. She is taking all her medicines as reviewed with Madison. Family history includes a son who had a heart attack, a brother who had a stroke due to sugar diabetes, and an eldest sister who had a heart problem. She has never smoked. She has no known drug allergies.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fevers or chills. Reports feeling overly tired/fatigued. Weight loss of about 10 pounds gradually over a year.
Cardiovascular: Reports a heart murmur. Denies chest pain. Reports shortness of breath with exertion (walking too fast/long) or trying to drink a whole glass of water without stopping. Denies palpitations, rapid heartbeats, or skipped beats. Reports ankle swelling for about six months.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath with overexertion.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Reports severe leg pain in both legs for about a month. Uses a walker.
Neurological: Reports lightheadedness and dizziness, for which she takes meclizine occasionally. Denies passing out/syncope.
Skin: Not discussed.
Endocrine: Not discussed.
Hematologic/Lymphatic: Not discussed.
Allergic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Constitutional: Elderly, otherwise in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Normal S1 and S2, preserved with a normal rate and regular rhythm. There is a 4/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with mild radiation to the carotids. No significant volume overload today.
Neurologic: Gait is normal for age.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Cardiac murmur: Diana has a 4/6 systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border with mild radiation to the carotids. This is most likely representative of aortic stenosis, and her symptoms could be due to severe aortic stenosis. However, her S2 is relatively preserved, which would be more consistent with moderate. Some outside records note diastolic dysfunction, so it is possible she had an echocardiogram in the past. She does not appear significantly volume overloaded today.
2. PVCs: Her referral mentioned tachycardia. Her EKG today shows sinus rhythm with frequent PVCs, as well as an anterior septum infarct pattern. She does not have any significant palpitations. We will check an echocardiogram to assess overall cardiac structure and function. Depending on results and the severity of her aortic stenosis, we will need to consider an ischemic evaluation or possibly a heart monitor to assess the overall burden of the PVCs. At this point, she is asymptomatic, so we will start with the echocardiogram only. The doctor discussed the possibility of aortic stenosis, and if severe, a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) as a minimally invasive procedure, noting she would need to think about it given her age. Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) would not be a good option due to her age and medical history.
3. Hypolipidemia: Managed by her PCP. Due to bilateral leg pain over the last month, considering TAVR evaluation following echocardiogram; a statin could be indicated, and she might be able to stop her statin (simvastatin 20 mg) given her leg pain, age, and no history of coronary artery disease, to be discussed with her PCP. The doctor will send over echocardiogram results and recommendations.
4. Lightheadedness/dizziness: She is on meclizine for this. It is possible that some of her lightheadedness and dizziness is related to aortic stenosis, and we will do an echocardiogram. PVCs on her EKG could be contributing, but she does not feel palpitations. We will consider a monitor, but start with the echocardiogram first.
5. Medications: Continue amlodipine, lisinopril, and levothyroxine with no changes.
6. Follow-up: Schedule an echocardiogram to be completed today. Follow up in three to four weeks after the echocardiogram is done to discuss results and next steps.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hematuria and renal ultrasound evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kelly Wood is an established patient seen for a renal ultrasound because of hematuria. The patient states she passed what looked like two small stones last week after scheduling the appointment. For the past six weeks, she has had a few episodes of bright red urine the color of cherry Kool-Aid. Last week, she was constantly having to pee and it hurt something terrible, rating the pain as an 8 on a scale of 0 to 10. She reports that after passing those stones, things have felt a lot better. She is currently taking Alavert 10 mg a day and has no drug allergies. The doctor wonders if it might have been a bladder infection.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for current flank pain or tenderness in the lower back. Positive for recent urinary frequency, painful urination, and episodes of bright red urine. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: No flank pain. 
Genitourinary: Normal vaginal exam. 

RESULTS
Urine dipstick today:
- Leukocytes: Negative
- Nitrates: Negative
- Protein: Negative
- Ketone: Negative
- Bilirubin: Negative
- Glucose: Negative
- Color: Yellow and clear
- Urobilinogen: 0.2
- pH: 5.5
- Specific gravity: 1.020
- Blood: Trace amount, intact.

Renal ultrasound impression:
- Right kidney: 10 cm in length by 5 cm wide. No stones, masses, or hydronephrosis.
- Left kidney: 10.8 cm in length and 5 cm wide. There is a 6 mm left renal stone, non-obstructing.
- Post-void residual: 533 mL pre-void and 0 mL post-void.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Primary diagnosis: Hematuria.
- Secondary diagnosis: Chronic urolithiasis.
- The blood in the urine was due to the kidney stones; the patient passed two last week and the blood has nearly subsided. 
- One stone remains in the left kidney. Since it is not obstructing or causing pain, the doctor does not recommend any surgical intervention at this time.
- Formation of kidney stones cannot be attributed to a particular cause, but risk factors include dehydration, family history, certain foods, digestive tract disease, and certain medical conditions. The patient acknowledges she does not drink enough water and drinks more Mountain Dew than anything.
- Water intake: The doctor recommends drinking about half of the body weight in ounces of water a day (for the patient's weight of 250 pounds, this would be 125 ounces of water a day) and avoiding sugary drinks like Mountain Dew.
- Dietary recommendations: Avoid foods rich in sodium, oxalate, and animal protein. Consume ideally less than 1,000 milligrams of sodium a day and reduce the amount of beef, poultry, fish, and pork. Avoid foods high in oxalate (an organic acid found in plants that binds to minerals that stones are formed from), such as spinach, chocolate, beets, rhubarb, and soy products.
- Handout provided reviewing dietary recommendations and what to avoid.
- Return visit scheduled for next year, as long as there are no more issues like bleeding or pain. The patient can call the office sooner if she has any issues.
- Instructions given to go to the emergency room if she experiences any severe pain or bright red blood in her urine.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abnormal lab finding (low hemoglobin) and fatigue.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Stephanie is a 49-year-old female with a past medical history of congestive heart failure, kidney stones, and prior colonoscopy, presenting for an abnormal lab finding. Over the past couple of months, the patient has experienced fatigue and dizziness, feeling worn out even with walking a mile or going to work. The doctor wonders if it might be a thyroid problem. 

The patient denies blood in her stools, dark, tarry, or black stools, heavy menstrual bleeding, passing out, weight loss, or loss of appetite. She reports having a colonoscopy about three years ago that showed mild diverticulosis, with no issues since then.

Regarding her congestive heart failure and watching salt intake, the patient notes it has been more of a struggle recently due to traveling a lot (exploring mountains in Vermont and eating McDonald's cheeseburgers along the way). She has noticed some swelling in her legs, but nothing too extreme where she thought she should call. She denies shortness of breath or problems lying flat at night.

Regarding her kidney stones from a couple of years ago, she reports no recent flare-ups, no back or flank pain, and no blood in her urine.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
The patient endorses dizziness, fatigue, and seasonal allergies with a little bit of nasal congestion due to the changing seasons. She denies fever, chills, sore throat, or cough. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure is fine and heart rate is right where it should be.
General: Physical examination looks fine.
Heart: A 3/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard, which has been heard in the past.
Lower extremities: Trace to 1+ pitting edema in the ankles, which the doctor notes is probably from the salt intake.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (from about six months ago): Shows a low pumping function of the heart at about 45%, and moderate mitral regurgitation (corresponding to the slight heart murmur heard on exam).
Hemoglobin: Low at 8.2.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. New anemia: The doctor will send off some more labs and an anemia profile to see exactly what type of anemia they are dealing with, and to make sure it is not something else. The doctor is referring the patient back to the gastroenterologist for another evaluation (who will probably do an endoscopy and another colonoscopy).
2. Congestive heart failure: The doctor notes the patient is retaining a little bit of fluid. Start Lasix 40 mg once a day. Continue Toprol 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg a day. The doctor advises the patient to watch her salt intake, get a scale, weigh herself every day, and call if her weight starts to go up (as the doctor might need to give her more diuretic).
3. Kidney stones: Everything seems to be fine at this time. Continue to watch diet and stay hydrated (though the doctor acknowledges this might be a little difficult with the diuretic, to do her best). Give the doctor a call with any questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a woman who presents with right foot pain after an injury that occurred a couple of days ago while playing tennis. She was trying to volley the ball in a doubles game, got in front of another player, fell on top of her foot, and twisted herself around the player to catch herself. She was unable to continue playing, had to be helped from the field, and could not put weight on her foot. She thinks it could be a bone bruise. For treatment since the injury, she wrapped it with ace wraps from the clubhouse, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen, which helps a little bit before wearing off. She reports no numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in the right foot. She injured her left foot previously, not this foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Normal temperature, no mention of fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop heard on exam; regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Stridor appreciated; no wheezes or rales.
Gastrointestinal: No rebound tenderness or guarding on abdominal exam.
Skin/Head: Head appears symmetrical, mucosal membranes normal, not hot to touch.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation reported; sensation intact to light touch on exam.
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain, bruising of plantar and dorsal aspects, swelling, tenderness to palpation of the midfoot, positive piano key test of first and second metatarsals, warm to touch. Left foot exam normal.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1 F, oxygen saturation 100%, pulse 60 beats per minute.
General: Vitals look great.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, rub, or gallop.
Respiratory: Stridor appreciated, no wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound, no guarding.
Head/Skin: Head looks symmetrical, mucosal membranes normal, not hot to touch.
Right Foot: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects, associated swelling. No pain when midfoot is touched, but tenderness to palpation of the midfoot and positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch. Neurovascular exam shows capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, and sensation intact to light touch.
Left Foot: Normal, appropriate capillary refill, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot showed subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment:
- Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to one of the second metatarsal bones near the top of the foot).

Plan:
- Surgery is recommended to place the bones in proper positions using plates and screws to help prevent further complications (such as poor bone alignment, poor ligament healing, loss of the arch/flat-footedness, and arthritis). The patient expressed fear of surgery, and the doctor explained it is a day surgery where she can go home the same day.
- An MRI will be ordered to further assess the fracture and any injury to the ligaments at the top of the foot.
- Post-procedure: The patient will be in a cast and use crutches, unable to use the foot for 6 to 8 weeks. She will not be able to drive and will need someone to take her home. She will follow up in the clinic in about a week. 
- The patient is out for the rest of the tennis season.
- Physical therapy is recommended after surgery to strengthen muscles.
- The medical assistant will provide paperwork regarding surgical risks (bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) to review with the patient.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after inferior STEMI and new stent placement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female with a history of coronary artery disease (status post RCA stent in 2018), hypertension, and diabetes, who presents for follow-up after experiencing an inferior STEMI requiring another stent. The patient reports it was a real shock, as she thought everything was fine after her last heart attack, but she started having horrible, unremitting chest pain similar to her first heart attack, leading her to the emergency room where she received a new stent. The doctor notes the symptoms might be acid reflux, though he is not sure. Currently, she denies current chest pain or shortness of breath. She is able to exercise, walking her dog every day for 1.5 to 2 miles. She reports her legs have been a little swollen since being sent home from the hospital. She is able to lie flat at night, though she always uses a couple of pillows and notes she may have had to sit up a little bit more, but considers it mostly normal. She is able to afford her medications with good insurance and is taking them as prescribed. Regarding her diet, she has been less strict with salt intake, admitting to loving pizza (with pepperoni) and fries, but states she will go back to watching her salt intake. For her diabetes, she has been watching her sugars to avoid going on insulin, taking metformin, and staying active by walking her dog.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Not discussed.
Eyes: Not discussed.
Ear, Nose, Throat: Not discussed.
Cardiovascular: Reports recent inferior STEMI with stent placement; denies current chest pain or shortness of breath. Noted leg swelling since hospital discharge. Uses a couple of pillows at night, possibly sitting up slightly more.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Genitourinary: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal: Not discussed.
Skin: Not discussed.
Neurological: Not discussed.
Psychiatric: Not discussed.
Endocrine: Monitors blood sugar, takes metformin.
Hematologic/Lymphatic: Not discussed.
Allergic/Immunologic: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good / patient is tolerating medication well.
Neck: No jugular venous distention appreciated. No carotid bruits appreciated.
Heart: Three over six systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: Lower limb edema noted, one plus pitting. Right radial artery cath site is clean, dry, and intact without hematoma. Right radial artery pulses are palpable.

RESULTS
EKG: Shows normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes anticipated after a STEMI.
Echocardiogram: Shows a reduced ejection fraction of 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary Artery Disease: History of CAD, status post recent inferior STEMI and new stent.
   - Continue aspirin 81 mg daily.
   - Continue Brilinta 90 mg twice daily.
   - Continue high-dose statin (Lipitor) 80 mg daily.
   - Continue Toprol 50 mg daily.
   - Refer to cardiac rehab for education and exercise confidence.
2. Newly reduced left ventricular dysfunction and moderate mitral regurgitation: Pumping function is concerning, but given history and quick cath lab intervention, the muscle is likely stunned and expected to improve over time with medication compliance.
   - Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
3. Acute heart failure (due to fluid retention / lower limb edema):
   - Prescribe Lasix 40 mg once a day.
   - Add Aldactone 12.5 mg daily.
   - Obtain labs.
   - Repeat echocardiogram in about 2 months.
4. Hypertension: Blood pressure seems fine.
   - Nutrition counseling referral to discuss diet options, reducing preserved meats like pepperoni, and finding alternatives.

Follow-up of chronic problems (arthritis, gout, reflux) and new reports of morning vomiting, abdominal pain, and bloating.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Anna is a 44-year-old female with a past medical history of arthritis, gout, and reflux, presenting for a follow-up after about six months. 
Regarding her arthritis and right knee, she reports doing well, noting that physical therapy went really well, and she has been doing pilates and lifting weights. She is walking about a mile to a mile and a half a day, has built her strength back, and feels joint pain is going away. 
Regarding gout, she had an episode in her right first big toe about two months ago, but is doing well now as the medication helped it go away. She is taking allopurinol with no issues and reports no further flare-ups. 
Regarding reflux, she was placed on omeprazole and instructed to make dietary modifications. She started making dietary modifications, though she has not cut out the stone quite yet. She reports still having some episodes and throwing up (actually vomiting) in the mornings. The doctor thinks it could be a stomach ulcer. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Endorses nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constant bloating. 
Last bowel movement was about two days ago, which was normal with no blood. 
No weight loss noticed. 
No fever or chills. 
Denies other symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look quite good.
General/Cardiovascular: Heart sounds good.
Respiratory: Lungs sound good.
Abdomen: Some pain to the right upper quadrant upon palpation. No rebound or guarding. No peritoneal signs. 
Musculoskeletal: Right knee shows a little bit of an effusion, some slight pain to palpation, and some decreased range of motion. (The doctor notes findings on the belly exam raise concern about the gallbladder, and the right knee looks a little swollen due to known arthritis).

RESULTS
Autoimmune panel: Sent because of her age and history of arthritis and gout; results showed everything seemed to be fine.
Right knee X-ray: Shows no fracture, but shows residual arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Reflux, nausea, and vomiting: 
   - Order a right upper quadrant ultrasound to rule out any gallstones.
   - Check some labs.
   - Continue omeprazole 40 mg once a day and continue dietary modifications.
2. Gout: 
   - Condition appears controlled. 
   - Continue allopurinol 100 mg once a day. 
   - Order a refill of allopurinol 100 mg once daily.
3. Arthritis: 
   - Doctor is pleased with how the right knee is doing. 
   - Continue pilates and using the knee. Patient to report any issues to discuss further imaging or intervention.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Abigail is a runner who presents with right knee pain that has been going on for a while. She states she does jogs, 5Ks, and sometimes marathons, but has not been doing longer distances because her right knee starts to ache when running. The doctor wonders if it might be tendonitis. To manage the pain, the patient uses ice and ibuprofen, which previously helped when the ache occurred after running. The pain makes it hurt a little more with running and activity, and she reports it is worse towards the end of the day, aching in the afternoon once she is on her feet all day. She was previously referred to Dr. Sanchez by her primary care provider, Dr. Wood.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for family history of arthritis or immune diseases. Negative for numbness or tingling in the feet. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 120/60, heart rate 58, respirations 14, no fever.
Heart and lungs: Sounds good.
Lower extremities: Left knee movement feels normal. Right knee: no redness, no swelling; a small amount of effusion (fluid under/in the knee's joint space) is appreciated. Pain is reported on the outside of the right knee. Pushing the leg out against the doctor's hand causes no pain; pulling back causes no pain. Good pedal pulse. No numbness or tingling when feet are touched.

RESULTS
X-rays done earlier in the morning show well-maintained joint spaces of the right knee, no evidence of fracture, and when compared to the left knee, everything looks good with no signs of arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Knee sprain from overuse, seen sometimes in runners.
2. Take time off from active running for two weeks; no running for two weeks. Weight lifting, squats, and gym exercises are allowed, but the patient should get the first physical therapy appointment in so they can recommend the best exercises.
3. Medications: Take two Tylenol 500 mg tablets and two ibuprofen 200 mg tablets, three times a day, to help with pain and inflammation. 
4. Order physical therapy for the right knee to strengthen lower extremities, provide balance, and recommend good running exercises.
5. Follow-up in two weeks to assess improvement and potentially add additional activity.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abnormal renal ultrasound with an atrophic right kidney.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ashley James is a 14-year-old previously healthy female who presented for evaluation of an abnormal renal ultrasound showing an atrophic right kidney. The patient previously came home sick with severe right-sided stomach pain, initially thought to be appendicitis. She was seen by her doctor and treated for a stomach virus with fluids. The next day, her symptoms worsened, and further testing/ultrasound showed that one kidney was bigger. After seeing her primary care doctor briefly, she was taken to Jacksonville, where she was told that one kidney was not working at all, was atrophic, and much smaller than the other. Cysts were found on her kidney and ovaries, along with swollen lymph nodes and infection. After following up unsuccessfully with her unavailable primary doctor, she went to Atlanta and stayed for four days, where she was seen and treated. Since then, her vomiting has resolved, but she still complains of stomach pain and burning, especially when eating or drinking certain items like soda. 

She has a history of being hospitalized three or four times at age four for infections, treated with fluids and antibiotics. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: No acute distress. 
Gastrointestinal: Complains of stomach pain and a burning sensation, especially when eating and drinking certain items like soda. No recent vomiting.
Genitourinary: Complains of burning when urinating, especially with carbonated drinks. Sometimes finds it hard to start urinating. No blood noticed in urine. 
Other systems not fully reviewed were within normal limits except as noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Well-appearing female, alert and oriented, sitting comfortably in a chair, no acute distress.
Heart: Sounds great.
Lungs: Sounds great.
Otherwise within normal limits.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Ashley's kidney functions and blood pressure look good. She is at a higher risk for developing high blood pressure and proteinuria.
- Right kidney is smaller, making the left kidney work harder and appear bigger; to be monitored with no immediate intervention needed today.
- Annual monitoring recommended: renal ultrasound to monitor kidney size and function, urinalysis to check for protein and blood, and blood pressure checks.
- Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen; use Tylenol instead.
- Stay well-hydrated during activities (softball, potential drill team) to avoid dehydration and strain on kidneys; recommended at least 2 liters of water per day.
- Maintain a healthy diet and active lifestyle.
- Future follow-up can be with her primary care physician or an adult nephrologist closer to home.

Right knee injury.

Sophia is a female who presents with right knee pain after slipping on her kids' backyard trampoline about four days ago. She tried taking ibuprofen and putting ice on it, which helped a little bit. The doctor thinks it could be a dislocated kneecap.

Not discussed.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Barbara is a 31-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes and asthma who presents with abdominal pain for the past one week. The patient guesses that drinking too much coffee lately (specifically venti nitro cold brews from Starbucks) might have triggered her gastritis, and the doctor thinks it could be a stomach ulcer. The patient also mentions she has been eating a lot of spicy food lately, which she thinks could be contributing towards her gastritis, and the doctor recommends cutting back on spicy food while it is hurting. The pain is gradually increasing in severity and is located on both sides of her upper abdomen. The pain spikes when she works out, such as when she jogs or goes for a run. The patient has experienced nausea on and off (about three times in the past week) and has vomited a couple of times. She reports no fever. The patient also has a moderately heavy history of alcohol use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever. Positive for nausea (about three times in the past week) and vomiting (a couple of times). 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart exam: Grade 3 out of six systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam; otherwise normal.
Abdominal exam: Mild tenderness in the epigastrium. Abdomen otherwise soft. No tenderness in the right lower quadrant whatsoever, and no significant tenderness in the right upper quadrant.
Lung exam: Mild end-expiratory wheezes, very faint; otherwise normal with excellent air movement.
Overall: Pretty normal physical exam for the most part, unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Abdominal pain: Acute gastritis, probably related to caffeine intake and spicy food, along with a moderately heavy history of alcohol use. 
- Cut back on alcohol to less than two or three drinks a week.
- Cut back on caffeine and spicy food.
- Prescription for Zantac to be taken twice a day as needed for acid and pain.
- Order labs: urinalysis, urine pregnancy test, CBC, and comprehensive metabolic panel.
2. Type 2 diabetes: 
- Continue metformin, but adjust the dose: increase the morning dose to 1000 mg and keep the evening dose at 500 mg (metformin 1000 mg in the morning and 500 mg in the evening).
- Continue to check blood sugars and track them.
3. Asthma: 
- Continue Flovent daily to decrease frequency of attacks.
- Continue albuterol as needed for wheezing.
Follow-up: Return in four weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female with a past medical history of type 2 diabetes who presents for evaluation of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer. She reports feeling pretty good, though depressed about the diagnosis. She initially sought medical attention due to severe pain and bleeding. The doctor wonders if it might be fibroids. Review of symptoms is positive for constipation and weight loss, but negative for vomiting. She reports no children and has never been pregnant. Menarche was at age 13, and menopause was at age 28. She has not taken any oral hormone replacement therapy and reports no history of endometriosis. Family history is non-contributory as the patient was adopted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for severe pain, bleeding, constipation, and weight loss. Negative for vomiting. (Other systems not discussed).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Slight tenderness to palpation of the left lower quadrant; no rebounding or guarding. 
Pelvic/Vaginal: No external lesions on the labia. Vaginal vault is within normal limits. Cervix is pink without lesions. Bimanual exam appreciates a left adnexal mass; no masses on the right.

RESULTS
Abdominal CT shows a 3-centimeter left ovarian mass with associated localized lymph node involvement. There is no evidence of gross peritoneal or metastatic disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Newly diagnosed ovarian cancer, most likely ovarian cancer, estimated as stage 3A disease based on lymph node involvement (doctor's assessment).
- Order blood tests including CA-125, hCG, AFP, and LDH to help determine the tumor type.
- Refer the patient for genetic counseling and testing to check for a genetic predisposition for developing ovarian cancer.
- Treatment plan involves surgery (hysterectomy, removal of both ovaries, and lymph node dissection) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and taxol. Depending on the surgery, intraperitoneal chemotherapy may be considered.
- Prognosis: The doctor states the patient has a favorable prognosis, noting she is still young and healthy, though a final pathology report is needed for a definitive answer.

Right ankle pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a woman who presents with right ankle pain after slipping and falling on ice yesterday while taking out the trash. She reports hearing a pop when she fell and was initially unable to walk on the foot at all; a visiting friend helped her inside. Today, she is able to put a little bit more weight on it, though she is still limping. She rated her current pain as a 4 out of 10 with ibuprofen, and states the pain is a 6 out of 10 without ibuprofen. She iced it last night, kept it elevated, and took ibuprofen last night and this morning, which helps with the pain. The doctor noted a possibility of a torn Achilles, though the final assessment notes a lateral ligament complex sprain. She has never injured this right ankle before, though she has a history of many injuries to her other ankle and played soccer in college and intramural soccer currently. She has not been able to play since the injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the right foot.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals look good. Focused exam of the right ankle reveals ecchymosis or bruising over the lateral malleolus, associated with edema or swelling of that area. Positive for tenderness to palpation of the anterolateral soft tissue. No laxity on anterior drawer and inversion stress. No bony tenderness on palpation to the foot or ankle area. Neurovascular exam of the right foot shows brisk capillary refill of less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, and sensation intact to light touch, consistent with the left side.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right ankle showed no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right ankle pain / right ankle sprain of the lateral ligament complex, more specifically the anterior talofibular ligament (stretched when she fell).
- Keep leg elevated when seated and continue to ice.
- Patient will be given an air cast to help stabilize the ankle.
- Prescribe crutches; patient is instructed to stay off the leg for now and start walking on it as tolerated in a couple of days.
- Continue to take NSAIDs or ibuprofen as needed for pain, inflammation, and swelling.
- Symptoms should significantly improve over a few weeks.
- Follow-up appointment scheduled in 14 days (2 weeks).
