He reports no blood in any place, no blood in stools, no vomiting, no vomiting blood, no coughing up blood, and no unintended weight loss. He reports no chest pain or shortness of breath. The doctor suggests it might be a hiatal hernia, but is not sure. 

For his diabetes, he takes metformin 500 mg twice a day. He feels he is doing great, taking his meds, sticking to them, and feeling pretty good otherwise. He checks his blood sugars in the morning about 80% of the time, and the numbers are looking okay and within the targeted range. He reports no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or other side effects from metformin. 

For his high blood pressure, he takes Norvasc and checks it about once a week or more. He reports the lower numbers are every once in a while a little higher, but usually close or on range. He notes he is low on Norvasc and requests a refill.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for coughing, vomiting, vomiting blood, coughing up blood, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, diarrhea, and other side effects from medications.

Neck: Fine, no swelling, thyroid feels normal, no masses, no lymph nodes, no carotid bruit.
Throat: Looks okay, no masses, no swelling seen, no redness.
Lungs: Clear.
Heart: Normal, no murmurs.
Abdomen: Epigastric tenderness in the right epigastric area where pressed; no masses or significant swelling felt.
Back: Normal.
Extremities: Normal.
Neurological: Fine.
Blood pressure in office: 120/50.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Difficulty swallowing: The doctor is concerned the patient may have a narrowing in his throat/esophagus (stricture).

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Acne on the face.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kayla Ward is a 14-year-old female (DOB 4/28/07) presenting for a new visit for acne located on the face, accompanied by her mother. The acne started about two years ago and is present most every day. It is not too bad on the chest or back. She has been using Persa-Gel and washing regularly, which she thinks has been somewhat helpful, though the mother notes it does not seem to help as much as they wanted. The patient's skin care routine involves wiping her face with water and a washcloth in the morning (or using an ELF facial cleanser if she feels really greasy), and at night using an ELF facial cleanser called the Super Clarity Cleanser, followed by a toner and Persa-Gel. The patient notes that today is an average/good day. The mother notes that the biggest flare probably occurred when she started school sports in the fall, just with all the sweating. The patient reports no flares with her periods, and her periods have been regular for about two years. There are no associated symptoms including itching, bleeding, or pain. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for itching, bleeding, or pain associated with the acne. Regular menstrual periods for about two years. All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Full exam performed today, except for under the underwear and under the bra. 
- Skin: Multiple benign nevi on the trunk and extremities (arms, legs, back, and abdomen), meaning they all look normal with no worrisome features. Scattered skin colored papules. Open and closed comedones. Erythematous papules on the face, primarily on the forehead and with also some on the central cheeks and chin. The chest and back are relatively spared.
- Remainder of the examination is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Assessment: Mild to moderate acne, mostly comedonal with a small inflammatory component. The doctor also thinks it could possibly be rosacea. Multiple benign moles on the arms, legs, back, and abdomen.
- Plan: 
  - Start with a topical therapy first.
  - Morning: Wash face with a mild cleanser, then use a moisturizer labeled "noncomedogenic" with sunscreen SPF 30 or higher. 
  - Evening: Wash face with the same cleanser and allow it to dry. Apply adapalene 0.1% cream in a thin layer to the areas where she generally gets acne. Start using this a few nights a week and slowly work up to using it every night. (Note: If adapalene is very expensive or not covered by insurance, she can try a different gel over the counter). Follow with Clean & Clear Persa-Gel in a thin layer where she generally gets acne, and then a noncomedogenic moisturizer. 
  - Sun protection: Topical retinoid will cause some sensitivity, so she needs to wear sunscreen when outside. It may also cause some dryness or irritation. (Patient currently wears SPF 30 sunscreen in the summer).
  - Follow-up: See if there is any progress over the next six months and follow up at that time. Call the office if there are any questions or concerns before the next visit.

He has tried Tylenol, ibuprofen, and a little ice, but reports they do not really help (the pain comes right back as soon as the medications wear off, and he did not notice the ice helping much). He denies any recent fever along with the elbow pain.

Musculoskeletal: Right elbow pain, worse with movement, better with rest. Otherwise, review of systems is negative as discussed.

Cardiovascular: Grade 3 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam. Otherwise normal cardiovascular exam.

- Rest the right arm as much as possible.
- Stop tennis for the next four to six weeks.
- Avoid repetitive stress in the right arm.
- Ice the right elbow for 20 minutes at least three times per day.
- Provide a brace for the right forearm (given by the nurse before leaving).
- Prescribe Ultram 50 milligrams once per day for pain.
- Follow up in four weeks to reevaluate the elbow, consider additional imaging if needed, and possibly refer to physical therapy depending on progress.

- Increase Metformin to 1,000 milligrams twice a day (previously 500 mg twice a day).

Hospital follow-up after an anterior STEMI, status post drug-eluting stent to the LAD, with newly reduced ejection fraction and moderate mitral regurgitation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Russell Ramirez is a 45-year-old male with a history of CAD s/p prior RCA stent in 2018, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus who presents for hospital follow-up after an anterior STEMI, now s/p drug-eluting stent to the LAD, newly reduced ejection fraction of 35%, and moderate mitral regurgitation. He reports feeling tired every now and then, but otherwise feels pretty well. The doctor suggests it might be anemia, though not sure. He reports no chest pain or shortness of breath. He has been doing short walks around the block and light housekeeping. He sleeps with two pillows, which is normal for him, and denies trouble sleeping or laying flat. He denies leg swelling. He is able to afford his medications through his plant insurance and is taking them as prescribed to prevent his stents from closing up. He is trying to watch his salt intake and change his diet, noting the hospital told him his heart pumping function is a little low and he might keep fluid on his legs if not careful; he notes it will be hard because he likes pizza, but understands he needs to cut back on salty foods to help his heart function and return to activities like walking trails and photography.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for chest pain, shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and lower extremity edema. Otherwise, negative except as noted in the HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base, pretty much the same as last year.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: No swelling or edema. Right radial artery cath site is clean, dry, and intact, without hematoma. Palpable radial pulse.

RESULTS
EKG showed normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes which are anticipated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease:
- Continue aspirin 81 mg daily.
- Continue Brilinta 90 mg twice daily.
- Continue high-dose statin (atorvastatin/Lipitor) 80 mg daily.
- Continue toprol 50 mg daily.
- Refer to cardiac rehab for education and exercise confidence.

2. Newly reduced left ventricular dysfunction and moderate mitral regurgitation:
- The doctor thinks his pumping function will improve in time, noting the heart muscle is likely just stunned and the patient is compliant with medications; the doctor expects it will recover.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
- Do not need a diuretic at this time (doctor's opinion).
- Add aldactone 12.5 mg daily.
- Get labs next week.
- Repeat echocardiogram in about two months.

3. Hypertension:
- Blood pressures seem fine at this time. Continue to monitor blood pressure periodically.
- The doctor anticipates he will tolerate the aldactone well.

Right shoulder injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 67-year-old right-handed male who presents with right shoulder pain after playing tackle football and getting tackled about 4 days ago (last weekend). He landed on his right shoulder in a weird way. He was able to finish the game, but the shoulder has been bothering him the past couple of days. The patient wonders if it might be a rotator cuff tear. He notes pain on the back side of the shoulder. He is able to grab a cup of coffee, but is trying to avoid lifting anything too heavy; he noted that reaching down and picking up a box in the driveway the other day was a little tough. He is able to lift up his shoulder to touch his ear, but it hurts a little bit. He has been taking Tylenol, which keeps the pain at the same spot but does not make it go down. His symptoms have been about the same since it happened. He denies any numbing or tingling in his fingers. He denies neck problems or injuring his neck. He denies any other joint problems (elbow and wrist are doing okay). He denies any past orthopedic injuries to that shoulder. Past medical history includes an appendectomy 3 or 4 years ago. He reports a slight headache after hitting his head a little bit during the incident, but denies passing out, fever, or chills.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Negative for fever, chills. Positive for a slight headache.
Neurological: Negative for numbness or tingling in the fingers, negative for loss of consciousness.
Neck: Negative for neck pain or injury.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for right shoulder pain. Negative for elbow or wrist pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 122/76, heart rate 82 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, no fever.
Cervical spine: No tenderness to palpation of the cervical spine; full range of motion.
Head: No trauma.
Right shoulder: No ecchymosis or bruising. Pain to palpation of the posterior shoulder at the acromioclavicular joint. Decreased abduction and adduction to about 90 degrees only. Pain with supination and pronation of the right arm. Palpable radial artery pulse.

RESULTS
Right shoulder x-ray: Showed an acute acromioclavicular joint fracture, specifically a small fracture of the acromion.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Right shoulder injury / acute acromioclavicular joint fracture (small fracture of the acromion). Surgery is not thought to be necessary.
- Place patient in a sling for now.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once a day (patient agreed to give this a shot for pain).
- Order a CT scan of the right shoulder to get a better look at how the joint looks.
- Refer to physical therapy to strengthen the shoulder in hopes of avoiding surgery in the future.
- Patient advised against playing tackle football while the fracture heals, and the doctor recommended avoiding tackle football in the future (suggesting flag football instead) due to weaker bones as we get older.

Ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis, right knee pain, and right leg swelling.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Tyler Nelson is a 79-year-old male (DOB: 03/06/1949) here for ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis. Last time he was here, he received a steroid injection in his right knee, which helped for about a couple of weeks. His right knee is still pretty painful and swollen. The patient reports that now the whole right leg is getting swollen. The doctor notes it might be gout, though is not sure. 
Current pain level is about a 3, but typically on a normal day it is around a 6. The swelling has been present for about two months (starting a couple of weeks after his last visit). Previously it was just the knee, and the whole leg was not swollen. He tried wearing compression socks a lot of the time, but they have not been helping much, though he notes they help to some degree. The swelling especially surrounds the knee. 
The pain and stiffness have slowed him down a little bit and made a few things feel too fast. It really hurts when he has been sitting for a while and tries to get up; he is so stiff getting up that he has to use a cane to get his bearings. After a little bit, it loosens up, but the first getting up is very difficult.
Medications: He takes Xeljanz XR 11 milligrams daily regularly, and Celebrex 200 mg daily which he started about 2 months ago. Both worked pretty good up until the swelling started again.
Diet: Patient notes he loves his salty snacks.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- General: Not explicitly detailed outside of knee/leg exam.
- Right knee and leg: Range of motion slightly diminished; patient reports it hurts when he tries to straighten it all down completely. The knee is hot to the touch, indicating inflammation. Pitting noted around the knee and ankle. Normal capillary refill in the toes. The area feels just kinda sore, like an old bruise, when pressed. 

RESULTS
- X-ray: Ordered for the right knee to see where all the swelling is coming from and to look for the cause of edema.
- CMP: Levels are good this time (patient needs to make an appointment for blood work for next time, as Xeljanz is a high-risk medication requiring checks every couple of months).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis with right knee pain, inflammation, and whole right leg swelling (possible gout noted by doctor as uncertain).
   - Performed fluid aspiration and steroid injection procedure today: Risks, benefits, and alternatives explained (including hypopigmentation, soft tissue atrophy, tendon ruptures, and transient hypoglycemia). Verbal consent attained. Right knee accessed through lateral approach with 3 mL of initially clear, then blood-tinged fluid. Prepped in standard fashion. Injected with 80 mg of triamcinolone and 1 mL of lidocaine. Procedure tolerated well with no complications. Post-procedure instructions given.
   - Ordered right knee X-ray.
   - Set up physical therapy.
   - If nothing helps, may need a surgery consult to see what can be done with the knee.
   - Edema management: Recommend reducing salt intake to help with water retention, propping feet up anytime (especially at night), and continuing compression socks. 
   - Advised patient to make an appointment with his primary care provider (PCP) if these measures do not help.
2. Xeljanz therapy (high-risk medication): CMP levels are good currently. Patient must make an appointment for blood work before the next visit.

Not discussed. (Note: Doctor mentions the nurse did the review of systems with the patient).

Physical exam is pretty normal other than mild wheezes in all lung fields.

IBS with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Ms. Edwards is a 32-year-old female seen for a return visit for IBS with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She reports flares of abdominal pain and nausea, which she experiences both in her upper and lower belly. She notes bowel movements are formed and occurring 2 to 3 times a day. She reports having more diarrhea after going out drinking with friends, typically consuming tequila, dark liquor (such as Patron, limiting brown liquor to two), or a martini. She often eats pasta with chicken alfredo at Friday's restaurant, which the doctor suspects contributes due to the fat and dairy content, though the patient states it does not normally bother her. She also reports having cramping and sharp pains and has been avoiding heavy foods, though she did eat some fried chicken today without major issue. She notes she has been doing better drinking water instead of sodas. She was previously instructed to start a low-dose daily fiber supplement and probiotics, but has not been using the fiber regularly. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert and cooperative, appears stated age.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No masses or organomegaly. Normal active bowel sounds.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Assessment: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional abdominal pain, aggravated by high stress, poor eating habits, and poor sleeping habits. The patient suspects lactose intolerance might be a factor.
- Dietary and Lifestyle Modifications: Encouraged reduction of triggers including greasy or fatty foods, spicy foods, dairy, and alcohol consumption. Encouraged portion control and drinking plenty of water. 
- Citrucel: Try Citrucel in tablet form, twice daily for regularity.
- Bentyl: Refill prescribed for Bentyl 20 mg. May use as needed for anticipated diarrhea when going out. - Follow-up: Plan to touch base via MyChart email in about one month to check in on symptoms, side effects, issues with Elavil, or if adjustments are needed. Prescriptions sent to the pharmacy.

- Respiratory rate: 18 breaths per minute
- Temperature: 97.9 degrees Fahrenheit
- Oxygen saturation: 100% on room air
- Pulse rate: Appropriate

Abdominal pain.

The pain waxes and wanes in severity, generally around a 4 or 5 out of 10, but sometimes gets as high as 7 or 8. It is usually a little worse after a meal; in the morning before she has eaten, it is not too bad. The pain is pretty localized to the right side, though it might radiate a little bit to the left. She reports some nausea and a little bit of heartburn, but no vomiting. She notes the area is a little tender if she presses on it, and certain positions seem to make it a little worse when the pain is highest. She reports no pain with urination, no blood in her urine, and no change in bowels (no diarrhea or blood in her stool). 

Due to nausea, her appetite is not quite as high, and she feels a little more fatigued over the last week. She has not eaten anything unusual and has not had any travel outside of Wisconsin recently. When asked about fevers, the patient reports she has had some chills, but no documented fevers. 

Regarding her migraines, she has not had a migraine recently. They usually respond to over-the-counter Excedrin migraine, and she uses sumatriptan as needed when it does not respond to the over-the-counter analgesic. Her migraines have been pretty rare. 

Regarding her hypertension, she checks her blood pressure about two or three times a week at home. The upper number is usually around the 120s or low 130s, and the lower number is usually in the 70s. She is still taking lisinopril 20 mg per day and is running low on her prescription.

Constitutional: Feels a little more fatigued over the last week; some chills, no documented fevers.
Eyes: Not discussed.
Ent: Not discussed.

Musculoskeletal: Not discussed.

Endocrine: Not discussed.

General: Looks a little bit elevated in blood pressure today (patient is noted to possibly be nervous).
Cardiovascular: Grade 3 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam; otherwise normal cardiovascular exam.

Remainder of exam: Pretty normal and unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

- Continue sumatriptan as needed for breakthrough migraine pain.
- Write a refill prescription for sumatriptan.
- Encourage avoidance of alcohol and caffeine binges and getting enough sleep.

- Continue lisinopril 20 mg per day.
- Write a refill prescription for lisinopril and send to pharmacy.
- Continue to check blood pressures daily.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Shirley Taylor is a 60-year-old right-handed female, referred by Dr. Jacob Ward, for evaluation of bilateral hand numbness and tingling. The patient reports having numbness and tingling for a few weeks now, which she thinks could be a pinched nerve. Symptoms have been present ever since a car wreck last December when she broke her wrists. She noticed the tingling and numbness more once they healed. Both hands have gotten worse over the last month. The patient is wearing wrist splints on both sides sometimes, though the right one is worse, and the splint seems to help. The right wrist was definitely in worse shape when she broke it than it is today. 

She also has some mild stiffness in her neck and hit her head during the accident, which was diagnosed as a contusion. On the right side, she notices the tingling and numbness from her middle and ring finger all the way up to her forearm. On the left, it is a bit more in the pinky and the ring finger, and not the middle. 

Symptoms are mainly just sore, and sometimes they throb. Overall, her hands feel weaker too, especially when she is using them. The tingling happens more, but when they hurt, it goes away and then the tingling is just dull. This occurs more so at night, and then comes and goes throughout the day. She does not experience a complete loss of sensation, though in general, they might be less sensitive than they should be, but she can still feel. She was given nerve pain medicine, but has not been taking it like she should.

Medical history is notable for chronic kidney disease, gout, hypertension, anxiety, GERD, and diabetes (patient notes she had pre-diabetes, but got it under control by changing her diet). Medications include carvedilol 25 mg twice a day for hypertension and lexapro 10 mg a day for anxiety. She is allergic to sulfa drugs, which causes her to break out in a rash. There is no history of thyroid issues.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Patient reports fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: Floaters.
Cardiovascular: Shortness of breath and leg swelling.
GI: Excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: Positive diabetes, always hungry.
Skin: Nail bed trenches, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: Gout, muscle pain.
Neurological: Paresthesia, bilateral hands.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Default normal neuro-physical exam with the following changes: Sensations normal except pin prick sensation diminished in the third and fourth fingers on the right, and the fourth and fifth fingers on the left. RESULTS
CT brain with and without contrast (2/5/21): No metastatic disease. No acute intracranial abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Question of bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome.

The doctor discussed the impression with the patient. The patient will be scheduled for EMG and NCV. If her symptoms do not resolve, they can consider a hand clinic referral for possible symptomatic injections or carpal tunnel release surgery, although she can pursue these through her current orthopedist. The doctor encouraged her to wear her splints and return for EMG and NCV.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents with left knee pain after an incident about a week ago while running and helping her 5-year-old niece take training wheels off her bike. The patient reports she fell and twisted her knee in a funky way, and heard a pop when she twisted it. She has been limping ever since, and the pain has not gotten better. She reports the pain is on both sides of the knee, but more so on the medial (inside) aspect than the lateral (outside). The pain started as a 4 out of 10 and is getting worse, described as a throbbing pain. She is able to bear weight on the left leg, though with a limp. 

The patient cannot take NSAIDs like Advil or ibuprofen due to a recent ulcer. She has been taking Tylenol, which helps a little bit, but wears off around hour one or two, and she takes it every four hours. She also wrapped the knee with kinesiology tape. 

The doctor initially wondered if it might be a meniscus tear.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Left knee exam reveals edema, effusion (fluid in the knee), and moderate range of motion. There is pain on flexion and extension of the knee. Lachman's test is negative. Valgus and varus stress tests are negative. The doctor notes tenderness to palpation on the inside (medial aspect) of the knee.

RESULTS
Left knee X-ray was normal, showing no fractures or bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment:
- Left knee pain, believed by the doctor to be a medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain caused by twisting the knee while running with her niece. The doctor does not believe anything is torn based on the physical exam.

Plan:
- Medications: Prescribed Tramadol 50 mg twice a day. Tylenol may be used as needed for breakthrough pain (noting liver safety precautions). Avoid NSAIDs due to recent ulcer history.
- Immobilization: Place the patient in a knee immobilizer to be worn for the next week to restrict movement, allow healing, and reduce inflammation.
- Ice: Ice the knee 3 or 4 times a day for 20-30 minutes at a time to help reduce swelling.
- Activity Modification: Avoid running for the next three weeks to allow the knee to heal. Expected recovery time to return to normal activities/running is about a month.
- Follow-up: Call the office if symptoms worsen in a couple of days to potentially consider further imaging such as an MRI.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male who presents for evaluation of a kidney stone. About a week ago, while working in the barn with horses and moving hay, he developed a sudden onset of pain in his right back. He initially thought it was from throwing hay, but he broke out into a sweat and became really nauseated. He saw his doctor, who ordered a CT scan and told him he had a kidney stone. The patient has never had a kidney stone before, though his father has had them in the past. The doctor wonders if it might be a pinched nerve. 

The pain radiated almost down to his groin, though not the whole way down. Since then, he has not had any more pain, and it has just been right about there. After he found out he had a kidney stone, the pain came a couple of times but did not last as long. He has been straining his urine using a little cup and does not see anything in there. He has not noticed any blood in his urine, and it has not been darker than usual.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs look good; there is no fever, and blood pressure and heart rate are fine.
Abdomen: No tenderness to pain to palpation of the abdomen; no rebound or guarding.
CVA: There is tenderness on the right side.

RESULTS
CT scan shows a stone measuring 0.5 centimeters located in the proximal right ureter (the duct that passes from the kidney down to the bladder). There is no evidence of hydronephrosis (which would mean the stone is obstructing the ureter causing swelling in the kidney).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone (0.5 cm in proximal right ureter).
2. Recommend pushing fluids to help facilitate urinating and passing the stone.
3. Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours for pain.
4. Can continue to take Tylenol between oxycodone for any breakthrough pain.
5. Continue to use the urine strainer until the stone passes.
6. Order a BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture to make sure everything else is okay and to see if antibiotics are needed based on the urinalysis for any type of infection.
7. Return visit in about one to two weeks, hopefully by which time the stone has passed. If not, further treatment such as lithotripsy (a shock wave procedure that breaks up the stone) can be discussed.

Chronic abdominal pain and changes in bowel habits.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 46-year-old male with a past medical history of GERD, anxiety, and depression who presents with chronic abdominal pain. He reports having pain on and off for about two years located in the mid-abdomen, just below the belly button. He describes it as a nagging feeling that sometimes bothers him and sometimes does not, and it gets a little better after having a bowel movement. A few months ago, he went to the ER and had a CT scan of the abdomen, which showed no acute abnormalities. 

More recently, over the past couple of months, the patient has developed changes in bowel habits, experiencing either constipation or explosive diarrhea. He feels he has more constipation, going about 3 to 4 times a week, and when he goes, the stool is hard. He notes that massaging his abdomen helps him eventually go. Regarding diarrhea, he reports it depends on what he eats, noting that sensitive foods like pasta with a creamy sauce trigger it, and it usually occurs just once before resolving. He denies blood in the stool, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, indigestion, or weight fluctuations. He has no prior history of abdominal surgeries or colonoscopy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Weight has been nice and pretty stable. No fever or chills.
HEENT: No jaundice observed in the eyes.
Cardiovascular: No history of ankle or foot swelling. No chest pain.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for chronic mid-abdominal pain, constipation, and occasional diarrhea triggered by certain foods. Negative for blood in the stool, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, and indigestion.
Skin: No jaundice observed. No excessive bruising or bleeding.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Appears well.
HEENT: Eyes and skin: No jaundice seen.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds are normal; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs noted.
Respiratory: Lungs are clear bilaterally.
Abdomen: Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Patient reports mild pain to palpation on the left side near the belly button. Examination reveals an increased stool burden in the colon and a slight enlargement of the liver (hepatomegaly) on the upper right side.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Abdominal CT (1/23/2020): Normal.
Previous labs (approx. 4 months ago): Slightly elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic abdominal pain and constipation/diarrhea: 
   - The patient's constipation and occasional diarrhea are attributed to diet and bowel habits (food sensitivities), and are not related to the liver enlargement, per the doctor.
   - Start a fiber supplement right away to help with constipation.
   - Increase water intake to at least 48 ounces a day.
   - Avoid foods that trigger diarrhea (e.g., pasta with creamy sauce).
   - Refrain from drinking alcohol.
2. Hepatomegaly and elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST):

   - Order repeat liver enzymes and additional lab work today.
   - Order a liver ultrasound (radiology scheduling will call this afternoon to set it up within the next two weeks; can be canceled if blood work is normal).
   - Recommended that the patient contact his primary care physician this afternoon to discuss his Crestor prescription and potential alternatives, as Crestor can cause liver toxicity.
3. Follow-up:
   - Return in 4 weeks to review test results, discuss fiber supplement and constipation management, and determine if further liver testing is needed.

Acid reflux.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle King is a 38-year-old female presenting for a new patient visit for acid reflux referred by Dr. Scott. The patient reports having acid reflux since she was around 12 years old, which has gotten worse over the past few years. She currently takes omeprazole 40 milligrams twice a day, which she has been on for about a year. While she feels it has helped somewhat, some days she eats something and it feels terrible. She reports burning in her chest and throat. Symptoms are worsened by stress and food choices, including spicy foods, sodas/carbonated beverages, citrus, and tomato-based products. She has not cut these foods out of her diet completely yet. She reports feeling stressed due to work as a paralegal, noting that stress and anxiety are big problems for her, and she has not had much of an appetite for the past two months. Her weight has been pretty stable. She denies difficulty swallowing, food or liquids getting stuck, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea, or rectal bleeding. Past medical history includes anxiety and seasonal allergies. Family history is significant for esophageal cancer in her maternal grandmother and acid reflux in her mother, who took a medication that coats the stomach lining. The patient thinks she may have had an upper endoscopy when she was younger, but not in the last 10 years. Other than omeprazole, she previously took ranitidine combined with omeprazole, which did help. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for difficulty swallowing, food or liquids getting stuck, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. Weight has been pretty stable, though she has not had much of an appetite for the past two months.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Normal physical exam per new patient template, except for well-healed abdominal surgical scars noted, which the patient reports was from surgery as a baby around one month old for twisted intestines.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment:
- Several-year history of GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), with recently poorly controlled symptoms despite omeprazole 40 mg twice daily. The doctor suggests it might be a hiatal hernia, though not sure.
- The doctor suspects that she likely has GERD with underlying functional etiology as well.
- Reassuringly, she has no unintentional weight loss and denies any dysphagia.

Plan:
- Dietary changes: Avoid trigger foods that can exacerbate GERD, including spicy foods, carbonated beverages/sodas, citrus, and tomato-based foods.
- Address stress and anxiety, which are triggers causing worsening of symptoms.
- Switch medication from omeprazole to Nexium 40 milligrams twice daily.
- Procedure: The doctor recommends an EGD (upper endoscopy) to look for potential causes of the GERD (such as ulcers or signs of precancerous or cancerous conditions, with biopsies taken if needed). The procedure involves sedation, passing a small camera through the mouth, down the throat, through the stomach, and ending in the small intestines. The patient can schedule this today at the checkout desk.
- Follow up in the office after the EGD to discuss results and review progress with dietary, stress, and medication changes.
- If her EGD is normal and her symptoms persist despite a trial of Nexium, the doctor can consider a trial of Protonix and obtain a pH-impedance study to rule out abnormal acid reflux exposure and to decipher between a functional etiology and hypersensitivity.
- Call the office if anything changes or if there are problems before the EGD and follow-up appointment.

Back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
John is a 61-year-old male with a past medical history of kidney stones, migraines, and reflux, who presents with back pain for the last four days. He reports the pain feels like the pain he had when he had kidney stones about two years ago. The pain started on the right side, moved over, and is now felt in the left side of his back. At first, the pain was coming and going, but for the last 48 hours, it has been a constant and pretty bad pain. He has taken Tylenol, which does not seem to help. He thinks he has blood in his urine, noting it looks a little off-color. When exerting himself (such as climbing three flights of stairs to his apartment or running to catch the bus), he feels a little dizzy, a little lightheaded, and feels a little bit more pain in his abdomen. He also reports some body aches because he thinks he is favoring his back when walking because of the pain. The doctor thinks the back pain could be a pulled muscle, but also suspects a recurrence of kidney stones.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Endorsing body aches from favoring his back.
Cardiovascular: Endorsing dizziness and lightheadedness with exertion. 
Respiratory: Not discussed.
Gastrointestinal: Endorsing abdominal pain with exertion. Acid reflux has been pretty good with diet, though he has been ordering take-out and fast food recently due to pain.
Genitourinary: Endorsing blood in the urine (looks a little off-color). 
Neurological: Migraines have been doing well with Imitrex; no issues reported. Diligent about taking meds.
Allergies: Not discussed.
Medications: Diligent with Imitrex for migraines. Taking Tylenol for pain without relief. Taking Protonix 40 mg a day for reflux (needs a refill).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure is a little high today, which the doctor notes is probably because he is in some pain.
Heart: Sounds nice and clear.
Lungs: Clear.
Abdomen: Feels a little tender; tenderness on palpation of the right lower quadrant.
Back / CVA: CVA tenderness on the right-hand side (tender when pounded on).

RESULTS
Creatinine: Drawn upon arrival and is up slightly, which the doctor notes might suggest a little bit of an obstruction there of one of the stones.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

   - Continue Protonix 40 mg a day; order a refill as requested by the patient.
Follow-up: The nurse will help get the CT scan scheduled, and the doctor will be in touch in a day or so. Patient is instructed to call if symptoms worsen.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Numbness and tingling in both hands.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 60-year-old right-handed male referred for evaluation of numbness and tingling in both hands, which has been present for a few weeks and has really gotten worse over the last month. The patient relates the onset/noticeability to a car wreck last December where he broke both hands and hit his head (resulting in a head contusion). The right wrist was definitely in worse shape after the accident. 

Symptoms involve both hands. On the right side, tingling and numbness extend from the middle and ring fingers all the way up the forearm. On the left side, symptoms extend from the pinky and ring fingers. The hands are mainly sore, sometimes throbbing, and feel weaker, especially when using them. The tingling happens more when they hurt, and when the pain goes away, the tingling is dull. Symptoms are felt more so at night, and come and go throughout the day. The patient reports no complete loss of sensation, though hands may be less sensitive in general. He was given nerve pain medicine but has not been taking it like he should. He also notes mild stiffness in his neck.

The patient is currently taking Coreg for hypertension and Lexapro for anxiety. He had prediabetes, which he got under control by changing his diet. No history of thyroid issues.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: Floaters.
Cardiovascular: Shortness of breath and leg swelling.
GI: Excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: Always hungry.
Skin: Nail bed changes, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: Gout and muscle pain.
The remainder of the review of systems is negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurologic examination:
- Sensation: Normal, except pinprick sensation diminished in third and fourth fingers on the right. Sensation is decreased in fourth and fifth fingers on the left.
- Reflexes: 1+ and symmetric; 2+ knees; toes are downgoing bilaterally.
- Tinel sign: Positive at both wrists and both elbows.
- Rest of exam is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- The doctor states the patient has bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, or potentially, this could also be bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome. The doctor notes the symptom presentation suggests bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, as the nerves in the wrists are aggravated by past trauma, causing the pain and tingling described.
- Plan: Schedule an EMG test (nerve test) to measure responsiveness of nerves and pinpoint where the issues are coming from.
- Patient to return for a follow-up visit after tests are complete.
- If symptoms persist, consider a referral to the hand clinic, possibly for injections or carpal tunnel release surgery, or alternatively refer to an orthopedist for the same treatment.
- Patient to continue wearing splints.

Headache.

She denies any fever or visual changes (such as wavy lines or spots in her vision). She has had headaches like this before, and states this is not the worst headache she has ever had. She denies any history of trauma, falling, or hitting her head, and believes it is just stress. She works a lot on the computer for work and does not really get the opportunity to take breaks every hour. Regarding her diabetes, she has not been checking her blood sugars. She is still taking her metformin 500 mg twice a day. She has not been eating well because of stress over the last week and has not been exercising for about the past week due to the headache making her feel uncomfortable and preventing her exercise, though generally she has been doing better.

Negative for fever and visual changes (wavy lines or spots). No other systems discussed.

Not discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Adult hydrocephalus follow-up, 3 months post shunt surgery.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christopher Watson is an 86-year-old male returning in follow-up for adult hydrocephalus, his first visit since undergoing shunt surgery on August 1st, 2020. The doctor has followed him since May 2020 when he first presented with 8 to 10 years of progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control. A diagnosis of adult hydrocephalus was established with a spino catheter protocol in June 2020, and a Medtronic Strata programmable shunt in the ventricular peritoneal configuration was placed at level 2.0 on August 1st, 2020. 

Mr. Watson and his daughter, Theresa, report that he has not been sick or hospitalized since the surgery. Regarding his symptoms, his walking has improved; he is now able to walk to the dining room just fine, which he could not do before surgery, though he still has times where his daughter has to help him. His bladder control improved somewhat after surgery but now seems to have leveled out, and he is wearing diapers. There are no issues with sores from wearing diapers, and no decreased or painful urination. Regarding cognition, the patient and his daughter feel he is better, and he does not feel lost when talking to someone anymore. His sister Hannah summarized it best by saying, "I feel like I can have a normal conversation with him again." The doctor mentions it might be a vitamin B12 deficiency, but is not sure. The patient reports no headaches, no pain where the shunt is, and no pain in his belly.

The patient asks if he will be able to drive again. The doctor thinks at this point it is unlikely that his movement speed will improve to the level needed to pass the driver safety evaluation, but notes that he occasionally has patients who surprise him by improving over a 9 to 12 month range, which definitely could happen for the patient. The doctor states that the patient could enroll in a driver safety program preemptively without a recommendation.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Significant for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.
GU: Significant for urinary incontinence and wearing a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased or painful output.
Neurological: Significant for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations.
Psychiatric: Negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 124/80, heart rate 64, respirations 18, weight 174 pounds, pain 0 out of 10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative man able to converse easily, though his daughter adds some details.
Shunt site: Clean, dry, and intact with a confirmed setting of 2.
Cognitive testing: Tested for recent and remote memory, attention span, concentration, and fund of knowledge. Scored 26 out of 30 on the MMSE when tested with spelling and 25 out of 30 when tested with calculations. Able to get two of the three memory words with cuing, and the third with multiple choice (a slight improvement over his initial score of 23 out of 30 with calculations and 24 out of 30 with spelling, where he previously was unable to remember any memory words with cuing and only one with multiple choice).
Gait testing: Tinetti assessment tool used without an assistive device. Received a gait score of 6 to 8 out of 12 and a balance score of 12 out of 16 for a total score of 18 to 20 out of 28 (slightly improved from initial score of 15 to 17 out of 28).
Cranial Nerves: Pupils equal. EOMs intact. Face symmetric. No dysarthria.
Motor: Normal for bulk and strength.
Coordination: Slow from finger-to-nose.

RESULTS
Head CT scan from 10/15/2020 shows a frontal horn span at the level of foramen of Monro of 4.6 centimeters with a third ventricular contour that is flat with a span of 10 millimeters. By the doctor's reading, there is a tiny amount of blood in the right front region with a tiny subdermal collection (this was not noticed or noted by the radiologist). There is also substantial small vessel ischemic change.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Adult hydrocephalus
- Gait impairment
- Urinary incontinence and urgency
- Cognitive impairment

Plan: 
- Leave the shunt set at level 2.0 for another 2 to 3 months before changing it, given the patient is improving and has no headaches or pain, despite the tiny blood fluid collection/subdermal collection seen on CT.
- Follow up in 3 months.

Left shoulder pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a very active individual who has been experiencing left shoulder pain for a few weeks now. The patient wonders if it might be bursitis. She has been renovating her basement and doing a lot of work associated with that, but she cannot think of any specific activity when the pain started and reports no direct or associated trauma, such as falling or hitting her shoulder. She has never had pain in that shoulder before, other than occasional minor aches and pains managed with Tylenol. The pain is isolated to the left shoulder. 

The patient experiences pain anytime she tries reaching for something or lifting anything, and she does not try to raise her arm over her head because it really hurts. The pain is present all the time and worsens with pressure, such as when trying to sleep at night. She is a side sleeper and cannot lay on her left side at all because it gives her a hard time and causes much discomfort. The pain increases when she sleeps directly on her left side compared to laying on her back. 

Without Tylenol, her pain level is a 7. She takes two extra-strength Tylenol every six to eight hours, which helps take the edge off and brings her pain level down to a 2 or 3. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals reviewed; everything looks good. 
Focused exam of the left shoulder shows limited active and passive range of motion. There is some tenderness of the greater tuberosity of the humerus. There is no tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints. Good hand grip bilaterally. Neurovascular exam of the left arm shows brisk capillary refill in less than three seconds, and motor and sensation are intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left shoulder shows no fracture or bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain: Symptoms are most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy (injury to the tendons that make up or attach to the shoulder muscles). 
- Order an MRI of the shoulder to make sure nothing else is going on.
- Refer for physical therapy for approximately six to eight weeks. 
- Continue to take Tylenol p.r.n. 
- If symptoms do not improve, consider a steroid injection of the left shoulder for potential relief. 
The doctor believes the pain will go away, noting that many patients are successful with physical therapy and taking a conservative approach. 
- Follow-up in about two weeks.

Hypertension and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 49-year-old male with a history of hypertension who was recently in the emergency room with high blood pressure and palpitations. The patient believes it was likely a panic attack or potentially low blood sugar, noting he had a few cups of coffee and no breakfast that day. He has not felt it again since. The patient reports having issues with blood pressure since he was young, and notes a family history of high blood pressure. He was put on a new combination medication (Benicar HCT, containing hydrochlorothiazide) by a new primary doctor about a month ago. He is also taking amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure every morning at home, and it has been running at about 146 to 155 lately. He is trying to back off on his salt intake and tries to walk on the treadmill when he can. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good. Abdomen is non-tender to palpation (patient reports no pain anywhere when pressed). Ankles and feet show no swelling.

RESULTS
Potassium level one week ago was 4.0.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Resistant hypertension, not yet controlled on current regimen (three medications maxed out).
- Add spironolactone to the regimen to help drop aldosterone levels and blood pressure.
- Discussed possible risks of hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone: electrolyte balance, dehydration (ensure proper hydration to avoid dizziness when standing up), potential for spironolactone to raise potassium (starting at 4.0), and potential for combination to lower sodium levels.
- Discussed side effects of spironolactone: dizziness, and rare risk of gynecomastia (tender chest, swollen or enlarged breasts); patient instructed to cut the medication and notify the doctor if this occurs.
- Emphasized importance of blood pressure control to prevent heart enlargement, heart failure, kidney failure, and strokes.
- Provided information on the DASH eating plan and recommended keeping salt under 2000 mg/day (ideally 1500 mg/day), increasing potassium, and using the website heart.org.
- Recommended routine treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days.
- Schedule a follow-up visit in two weeks to check blood pressure, electrolytes, and metabolic panel.
- If the new medication is not effective, next steps may include consideration of carvedilol (avoided due to potential for erectile dysfunction) or a referral to the resistant hypertension clinic to evaluate for secondary causes and potential procedures such as renal denervation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left-sided back pain and suspected kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Linda is a patient with a history of hypertension and diabetes who presents reporting about three days of constant left-sided back pain that is traveling a little lower toward the groin. She thinks she might have a kidney infection or a kidney stone, noting she has had kidney stones about twice before (this being her third time, though she hasn't had one in a while). She states it usually takes about three to four days to pass a stone. She has not passed this one yet. She reports seeing some blood in her urine this morning. She reports no fever, but does have some chills, cannot eat due to pain, and feels a little nauseous. She has been taking Tylenol and trying some ibuprofen, but it is not really working. 

For her hypertension, she is on 2.5 mg of Norvasc. She got a blood pressure cuff and reports top numbers usually in the 130s, sometimes 140s, and once 150, with bottom numbers between 70 and 80. She admits to struggling with reducing her salt intake, particularly regarding french fries, and expressed that some help with her diet could be helpful. 

For her diabetes, she takes 500 mg of metformin and checks her blood sugars before eating daily, reporting they have been pretty good in the low 100s.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, some chills, can't eat, feels a little nauseous.
Chest: No chest pain.
Cardiovascular: Known murmur.
Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath noted.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain (notes back pain is starting to go down into her groin).
Genitourinary: Able to urinate, saw some blood in the urine this morning.
Musculoskeletal: Left-sided back pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Not detailed.
Heart: Grade 2 out of six systolic ejection murmur (known about previously).
Lungs: Clear bilaterally, no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation of the abdomen; no rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: CVA tenderness on the right on the flank (note: transcript mentions CVA tenderness on the right/flank while discussing patient's left-sided pain presentation).

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone: Patient has a kidney stone with possible inflammation around the kidney indicated by CVA tenderness. 
   - Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg, take every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain.
   - Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain.
   - Push fluids to help push the stone out and clear the kidneys.
   - Provide a strainer to strain urine to see if the stone is passed.
   - Refer to urology, to be seen even if the stone passes in the next couple of days, due to recurrent kidney stones.
2. Hypertension: Blood pressures look good; keep on Norvasc 2.5 mg with no changes.
3. Diabetes: Keep on metformin 500 mg.
4. Diet/Nutrition: Refer to nutrition/a dietitian to help with diet management and reducing salt intake.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction and pre-op evaluation for right knee replacement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 74-year-old female with chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction, seen for a follow-up visit. Earlier in the spring, her BNP was 3,000 in March and increased to 6,000 in April alongside increasing dyspnea. Her diuretic was changed from furosemide to torsemide 20 mg by mouth daily, and her lisinopril was increased to 10 mg daily in March. She is not currently on a potassium supplement. 

Since her last visit in April, she has lost about 3 to 3.5 pounds, which she and the doctor note is positive, though some may be water weight. She reports oxybutynin is helping her urinary urgency. She reports having leg cramps the other day when she woke up with both legs cold from a ceiling fan; she drank about 4 ounces of pickle juice and the cramps went away. The doctor notes it might be restless legs syndrome, and advises her to keep pickle juice in moderation due to salt content. For heartburn, she previously took Prilosec for about two weeks back in January after stopping another medication, and has not had problems since. She is overdue for a colonoscopy and expresses interest in having it done within the next 30 days before her husband's insurance runs out; the doctor notes this can be done locally and will not delay her knee surgery scheduled for June 24th at East Metro.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: 3 to 3.5 lb weight loss since April.
Cardiovascular: No acute chest pain reported; chronic CHF. Leg cramps noted.
Respiratory: Breathing is non-labored.
Gastrointestinal: Heartburn resolved since taking Prilosec in January; bowel habits reported as good.
Genitourinary: Urinary urgency much better with oxybutynin.
Hematologic/Lymphatic: Anemia history; iron supplement use confirmed ("yes, everything is good").
Neurological: Leg cramps; possible restless legs syndrome suggested by doctor.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Lungs sound pretty good. Breathing is non-labored. Blood pressure is looking good.

RESULTS
- Hemoglobin: Doing great / checked, anemia stable.
- Potassium: 3.9, holding steady on torsemide.
- Creatinine: 0.7, indicating good kidney numbers.
- BUN: 23, noted by doctor as a tiny bit elevated, which can sometimes indicate dehydration.
- BNP: Results still pending from the test sent out to monitor heart failure (noted previous values of 3,000 in March and 6,000 in April).
- Blood glucose: 169 today (non-fasting); doctor notes it may need to be repeated for pre-op.
- A1C: 5.5 in March (doctor also mentions 5.1 in the assessment and plan section).
- Magnesium: Normal at 1.7; doctor notes desire to get it up to the 2-ish range to help stabilize heart muscle.
- EKG: Ordered to be repeated today.
- Chest X-ray: Not needed as she had one recently.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic CHF (mixed presentation): Had an exacerbation earlier in the spring. Switched from furosemide to torsemide, and symptomatically she is doing a lot better. Weight is down 3 to 3.5 pounds. Breathing is non-labored. Will repeat EKG today and continue current regimen. Creatinine is appropriate. Will consider adding a magnesium supplement twice daily to help get levels up to the 2-ish range for heart muscle stabilization.
2. Pre-op examination: Scheduled for right knee replacement on June 24th at East Metro. Will need to stop clopidogrel for a week prior to surgery. Pre-op check to be completed within two weeks of surgery during the first or second week of June. May repeat EKG today. 
3. Screening colonoscopy: Patient is overdue, with no family history of colon cancer. Patient requests it within the next 30 days due to potential changes in her husband's insurance. Doctor will put in a referral for county/local options (Dr. Martin at county surgical services or Valley Medical at Springfield) to be completed within the next few weeks; this will not delay her surgery.
4. Diabetes: A1c was 5.5 in March (noted as 5.1 in assessment dictation). No need for further A1c today, though she may need another one prior to surgery next month. Random blood sugar was 169 today (non-fasting), may repeat for pre-op.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic CHF exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an 82-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease who presents for a hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic CHF exacerbation. The patient reports that he was trying to watch his diet, but noticed his ankles were swelling, and then he got super short of breath and had to call 911. Paramedics placed him on a special mask, and in the ER, his blood pressure was super high at 200/90. The doctor wonders if it might be poor circulation. 

Regarding medications, the patient states he takes them most times, though sometimes he misses a dose or two. Regarding his diet, the patient admits to eating pizza and chicken wings at parties on the weekends with friends. The patient feels much better now after being in the hospital for a couple of days, where he received a water pill through his IV and oral medicine that made him go to the bathroom frequently, and he believes he is on different medications for blood pressure now. He has been following instructions since coming home because he does not want to go back to the hospital. He ordered a blood pressure cuff, checks it about every other day, and reports his blood pressure has been really good. He reports no shortness of breath, can get up and move around without trouble, has no problems sleeping, and has a good afternoon nap. He reports no chest pain at all since being home.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for shortness of breath, trouble sleeping, and chest pain. Trace lower extremity edema noted in physical exam.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/72, heart rate 79, respiratory rate 26 (noted as likely due to talking), O2 saturation 99%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Lower extremities: Trace of edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive Heart Failure: Exacerbation likely caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension. 
- Continue bumex 2 mg one daily.
- Continue to watch diet and avoid salty foods, cutting back on pizza and chicken wings.
- Weighself every day and call if weight gain is 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Referral to see a nutritionist for dietary education.

2. Hypertension: 
- Continue cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order a renal artery ultrasound to rule out secondary causes affecting the kidneys.

3. Chronic Kidney Disease (Stage 3): 
- Order more blood work labs to ensure tolerance of the regimen.

Follow-up in 3 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood pressure and concerns regarding kidneys.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a new patient referred by her primary care provider (PCP) due to uncontrolled high blood pressure and abnormal recent blood work noting something about her kidneys. Her PCP recently added medications, but the blood pressure remains hard to control. The patient states she feels fine most days and is busy at work, but she can tell when her blood pressure is high. She checks her blood pressure with an electronic arm cuff a few times a week; the other day it was as high as 170/90. Diet-wise, she admits to eating pizza, wings, and subs during football season, though she tries to cut down on non-game days. She takes Advil, Motrin, or Aleve just once in a while for knee or back pain, not every day. Alcohol intake consists of a couple of beers during the week and 1 to 2 on the weekends.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Headaches: Reports mild headaches only when her blood pressure gets really high; otherwise, no regular headaches.
Chest pain: None.
Shortness of breath: None, even with exertion.
Lower extremity swelling: Notices a little swelling if she is on her feet for a long time; otherwise, no.
Family history: Both parents have high blood pressure, and one parent had kidney disease.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygenation 98%.
Neck: No jugular vein distention, no carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard, with an extra sound noted.
Extremities: Small amount of 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnosis: Uncontrolled hypertension, suspected to be multifactorial. The doctor mentioned sleep apnea as a possibility ("It might be sleep apnea i'm not sure").
Plan:
- Keep a record of home blood pressure readings (taken at the same time every day if possible) and bring them to the next visit in three weeks.
- Decrease alcohol intake to about one or two a week.
- Be very judicious about decreasing salt intake; given a referral to a nutritionist to discuss diet changes.
- Stop taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as Advil, Motrin, or Aleve); use Tylenol for pain instead.
- Order a renal artery ultrasound to rule out narrowing in the blood vessels of the kidneys.
- Order a urine collection, morning aldosterone levels, renin levels, and a 24-hour urine to check for adrenal gland problems.
- Prescribe Cardura 4 mg once daily.
- Return in three weeks.
- The doctor will talk to the patient's PCP to coordinate treatment plans.
